title: Resting in the Two Turning Points of the Breath

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y1 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: ūrdhve prāṇo hy adho jīvo visargātmā paroccaret | utpattidvitayasthāne bharaṇād bharitā sthitiḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Bhairava answers: the supreme power, whose nature is to pour itself out (visarga), keeps sounding as the breath: prāṇa moving upward and out, jīva moving downward and in. By filling with awareness the two places where these movements arise, one comes to rest in fullness (bharitā sthitiḥ).
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh's notes (following the Kashmir Shaiva commentators) place the two points at the heart-centre, where the in-breath ends, and the outer dvādaśānta, about twelve finger-widths in front of the nose, where the out-breath ends. The verse itself only says 'the two places of arising'.

instruction: Breathe naturally and let awareness rest where the breath turns: inside after the in-breath, outside after the out-breath.

method.text: Breathe naturally. At the end of each in-breath, rest awareness for a moment at the inner turning point; at the end of each out-breath, rest it at the outer turning point. Do not stop, slow or lengthen the breath; meet the pause that is already there.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 24 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. If counting helps, an even four in and four out; otherwise do not count. No forced hold. Notice the natural brief turn at the top and bottom of each breath.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The two places where the breath turns: inside (heart-centre) and outside (space in front of the nose)
attention.secondary: The fullness of the pause itself

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The dharana's own map is two points joined by the path of the breath: the inner point where the in-breath ends and the outer point where the out-breath ends. The exact locations come from commentary (Singh's notes), not from the verse.
points: outer turning point: about twelve finger-widths in front of the nose (commentarial, 'outer dvādaśānta')

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Never hold or stop the breath for this door. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.

beats.title: Name the door
beats.script: This is Door 001: the two turning points of the breath. It is the first dharana of the Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra, verse 24.

beats.title: Geometry
beats.script: No shape to make. Sit, lie down, or stand, whatever is easiest. The map is two points: where the in-breath ends inside, near the heart, and where the out-breath ends outside, in front of the nose.

beats.title: Orientation
beats.script: Let the floor or the chair carry you. Eyes soft or closed. Turn attention toward the turning points, not toward the air.

beats.title: Breath
beats.script: Breathe naturally. If counting helps, four in, four out, six easy rounds. No forced hold.

beats.title: Attention
beats.script: Rest at the inner turn after each in-breath, and at the outer turn after each out-breath. Notice the pause that is already there.

beats.title: Reaction cue
beats.script: School image: scattered charge settles into fullness. A metaphor, not medicine.

beats.title: Adiyogi thread
beats.script: Verse 24: fill the two places where the breath arises with awareness, and rest in fullness. Do not stop the breath. Meet the pause that is already there.

beats.title: Exit / integrate
beats.script: Take one free breath without watching it. Open the eyes. Carry the sense of fullness into whatever comes next.

title: Not Turning Back from the Two Spaces

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y1 (cont.) (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: maruto 'ntar bahir vāpi viyadyugmānivartanāt | bhairavyā bhairavasyetthaṃ bhairavi vyajyate vapuḥ ||
dharana.rendering: O Bhairavī, when the breath, whether it has moved inward or outward, is not hurried back from the two spaces where it comes to rest, the inner and the outer, then in this way Bhairava's form shows itself through Bhairavī.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh describes the two spaces as the split-second pauses at the heart-centre and at the outer dvādaśānta. Singh calls the two pauses the outer and inner kumbhaka but describes them as split-second natural pauses that are only observed; this school follows that observational reading.

instruction: Breathe naturally and stay present in the small space after each in-breath and each out-breath, without hurrying on.

method.text: Breathe naturally. Notice the small space after the in-breath and the small space after the out-breath. Stay present in each space instead of hurrying attention back into the next movement. Do not hold the breath to make the space longer.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 25 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Let each pause last exactly as long as it naturally lasts; do not lengthen it on purpose. Never force the pause.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The two spaces where the breath rests, inside and outside
attention.secondary: The habit of rushing into the next breath, noticed and softened

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The verse names a pair of spaces (viyad-yugma), one inside and one outside, where the breath pauses. The practice is to stay in each space a moment longer before attention rushes on.
points: inner space: where the in-breath rests (commentarial: heart-centre)
outer space: where the out-breath rests (commentarial: outer dvādaśānta)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Do not convert this into breath-holding. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

beats.title: Name the door
beats.script: This is Door 002: not turning back from the two spaces. Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 2, verse 25.

beats.title: Geometry
beats.script: No shape to make. Any easy seat, or lie down. The map is a pair of spaces: one inside after the in-breath, one outside after the out-breath.

beats.title: Orientation
beats.script: Let the body be fully held by the floor or chair. Eyes closed or lowered. Face the two spaces.

beats.title: Breath
beats.script: Natural breath, about four in and four out if you like to count. Never force the pause.

beats.title: Attention

beats.title: Reaction cue

beats.title: Adiyogi thread
beats.script: Verse 25: by not turning back from the two spaces, inner and outer, Bhairava's form shows itself through Bhairavī. Do not hold the breath; just do not hurry away.

beats.title: Exit / integrate
beats.script: Let the breath go unwatched for one round. Open the eyes slowly.

title: The Opened Centre Where Breath Neither Leaves nor Enters

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y1 (cont.) (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: na vrajen na viśec chaktir marudrūpā vikāsite | nirvikalpatayā madhye tayā bhairavarūpatā ||
dharana.rendering: When the centre (madhya) opens out, the power that has the form of breath neither goes out nor comes in; as thought-constructs fall away in that middle, the state of Bhairava appears through her.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh and Wallis read this as a description of what happens spontaneously when the middle opens. Bäumer (as printed in The Mystery Within) translates it as an instruction ('The Energy of Breath should neither move out nor enter'); Wallis's concordance shows Dyczkowski reading it the same way. This school follows the spontaneous reading and never induces a stop of the breath.

instruction: Rest awareness in the still centre where the breath is neither going out nor coming in. Recognise the pause; never create it.

method.text: Rest awareness in the natural still centre where breath-energy is not rushing out or in. Recognise the pause rather than creating it. If breath pauses lightly on its own, witness it; never induce or prolong a stop of the breath.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 26 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Optional: a slightly longer out-breath (about four in, six out) while settling, then stop counting. No forced breath-hold. If the breath pauses on its own, witness it; do not strain into a hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The still point at the middle of the breath (madhya), where inhale and exhale meet and quiet
attention.secondary: Thoughts thinning on their own

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The verse points to one centre, the middle state where breath is neither going out nor coming in and thought thins. It is a point in experience more than a place in the body.
points: the middle (madhya): the still centre between out-breath and in-breath

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Never induce or prolong a stop of the breath for this door. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

beats.script: This is Door 003: the opened centre where breath neither leaves nor enters. Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 3, verse 26.

beats.title: Geometry
beats.script: No shape to make. Sit or lie in any easy way. The map is one point: the middle, between going out and coming in.

beats.title: Orientation
beats.script: Let the floor take your weight. Eyes closed or lowered. Turn toward the middle.

beats.title: Breath
beats.script: Natural breath. If it helps you settle, four in and six out, then stop counting. No forced breath-hold.

beats.title: Attention

title: Retained Breath and the Tranquil

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y1 (cont.) (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kumbhitā recitā vāpi pūritā vā yadā bhavet | tadante śāntanāmāsau śaktyā śāntaḥ prakāśate ||
dharana.rendering: When the breath-power is held (kumbhita), whether after it has been let out or after it has been drawn in, then at the end of that holding the power called 'the tranquil' (śāntā) reveals the Tranquil One.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: exhalation retained outside and inhalation retained inside; at the end of the practice the śakti is called śāntā. Wallis groups verses 24 to 27 as one breath technique, with this verse as its retention phase.

instruction: Observe only: read the verse and its classical description. This door is not practised.

method.text: Classical method: retention of the breath (kumbhaka) after exhaling or after inhaling, followed by resting in the tranquillity at the end of the retention.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Deliberate breath retention is not taught by this school. Breath-holding can bring dizziness, light-headedness or fainting and is not suitable for everyone, for example during pregnancy or for people with heart, blood-pressure or breathing conditions. Anyone who wants to learn retention should do so only with a qualified teacher and their own clinician's advice. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.

title: Rays Rising from the Root, Dissolving above the Crown

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y2 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)
numbering_variants.popular_lists: Old notes say some popular lists number a different technique as 5; that claim could not be traced to a named edition and is unverified.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: āmūlāt kiraṇābhāsāṃ sūkṣmāt sūkṣmatarātmikām | cintayet tāṃ dviṣaṭkānte śāmyantīṃ bhairavodayaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Contemplate her, the power, shining like rays of light from the root, becoming subtler than the subtlest, until she comes to rest in the 'end of twelve' (dviṣaṭkānta, the dvādaśānta above the crown); then Bhairava arises.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh glosses 'the root' as the mūlādhāra cakra and dviṣaṭkānta as dvādaśānta. The Mystery Within glosses the end point as the sahasrāra cakra. The verse itself says only 'from the root' and 'at the end of twelve'.

instruction: Rest attention at the base of the body and imagine a soft radiance rising along the centre line until it dissolves above the crown.

method.text: Rest attention at the base of the body, then imagine a soft radiance rising along the centre line, growing subtler and subtler until it dissolves in the space above the crown. Ordinary breath. Do not force heat, shaking, breath retention or dramatic effects.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 28 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Ordinary breath, about four in and four out if counting helps. No forced hold. Do not pump or push the breath to make the light rise.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: A fine line of light rising from the root and thinning toward the point above the crown
attention.secondary: The moment it dissolves

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The dharana's map is a vertical line of light rising from the root of the body to a point above the crown, growing finer until it dissolves.
points: root (Singh: mūlādhāra, base of the spine)
end of twelve (dvādaśānta), above the crown

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Visualisation only, with ordinary breath. If the practice brings agitation, heat, shaking or strong emotion, stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

beats.title: Exit / integrate
beats.script: Let the image go. Feel the weight of the body and the floor. Open the eyes.

title: Lightning Rising Centre by Centre

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y3 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: udgacchantīṃ taḍidrūpāṃ praticakraṃ kramāt kramam | ūrdhvaṃ muṣṭitrayaṃ yāvat tāvad ante mahodayaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Contemplate her rising like lightning, from centre to centre (cakra) in sequence, upward as far as three fists above the head; at the end there is the great dawning (mahodaya).
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh identifies the power as kuṇḍalinī and 'three fists' as the dvādaśānta. Singh contrasts it with verse 28: here the power climbs through the centres one by one, whereas in verse 28 it goes straight up.

instruction: Gently mark attention centre by centre up the central line, then rest in the space above the crown for a breath or two.

method.text: Gentle form: quietly mark attention centre by centre up the central line (base, belly, heart, throat, brow, crown), then rest awareness in the space above the crown for a breath or two. Contemplative tracing only; never try to produce rushes, heat or shaking, and never force sensation or breath.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 29 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Ordinary breath, about four in and six out if counting helps. No forced hold. Never use the breath to drive the image.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: Attention moving centre by centre up the central line to a point above the head
attention.secondary: Resting in the open space at the end

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a vertical line with stations along it, and a quick flash of light passing station by station to a point about three fists above the head.
points: successive centres (cakras) along the central line
three fists above the crown (Singh: dvādaśānta)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. This school teaches only a slow, gentle tracing of this dharana. If it brings agitation, strong sensations or emotion, stop, open the eyes and ground attention in the feet. People who have had strong reactions to energy-focused meditation should choose a breath or sound door instead (for example Door 001 or Door 015). If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Twelve Stations, Twelve Letters

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y4 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kramadvādaśakaṃ samyag dvādaśākṣarabheditam | sthūlasūkṣmaparasthityā muktvā muktvāntataḥ śivaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Twelve stations in sequence, each properly marked by one of twelve letters: attend to each in its gross, then subtle, then supreme form, leaving each behind in turn; in the end there is Śiva.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh's notes list the twelve stations (janmāgra at the level of the generative organ, mūla, kanda, nābhi, hṛd, kaṇṭha, tālu, bhrūmadhya, lalāṭa, brahmarandhra, śakti, vyāpinī) and pair them with twelve vowels (a ā i ī u ū e ai o au aṃ aḥ). The verse itself names neither the stations nor the letters: both lists are commentary.

instruction: Move attention up the centre line one station at a time: feel it coarsely, then subtly, then let it go and rise.

method.text: Classical method (Singh's notes): twelve stations from janmāgra to vyāpinī, linked with the twelve vowels, each contemplated in gross, subtle and supreme phases and then left behind. School simplification (flagged): move attention up a short midline sequence (pelvic floor, navel, heart, throat, brow, crown). At each station feel the coarse sense, then a subtler quiet, then leave it and rise. No phoneme placement, no forced breath-hold.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 30 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Equal inhale four, exhale four if counting helps. Keep the breath quiet and even. No forced retention.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: One station at a time: feel it coarsely, then subtly, then let it go and rise
attention.secondary: The release itself, each time a station is left

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a ladder of twelve stations, each paired with a letter, climbed and released one at a time through gross, subtle and supreme phases.
points: twelve stations in rising sequence (locations given in commentary, not in the verse)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. The school form is a simplification. It leaves out the vowel placements and the first commentarial station (janmāgra, at the level of the generative organ), and stops at the crown instead of continuing to the two stations beyond the body (śakti, vyāpinī). If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Filling to the Crown, Crossing the Brow-Bridge

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y5 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)
numbering_variants.previous_draft: The previous draft of Door 008 used Wallis Y8 = verse 34. Under Singh, verse 34 is dharana 11 (Door 011).

dharana.sanskrit_iast: tayāpūryāśu mūrdhāntaṃ bhaṅktvā bhrūkṣepasetunā | nirvikalpaṃ manaḥ kṛtvā sarvordhve sarvagodgamaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Having quickly filled [the body] up to the top of the head with that [breath-power], and having broken through by means of the 'bridge' made by contracting the eyebrows, make the mind free of thought-constructs; then, in what is above all, the all-pervading arises.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: fill the mūrdhānta with prāṇic energy and cross it with the bridge-like contraction of the eyebrows. Singh adds that the esoteric bhrūkṣepa technique 'was a closely guarded secret among the mystics and is now practically lost'. The Mystery Within's own rendering reads the 'breaking' as suspending the breath while concentrating at the ājñā cakra.

instruction: Observe only: read the verse and its classical description. This door is not practised.

method.text: Classical method: rapidly filling the body to the crown with breath-power, breaking through with a contraction of the eyebrows, and making the mind free of thought.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Forceful breath-filling, breath suspension and sustained brow contraction are not taught by this school. They can bring headache, dizziness or light-headedness. Do not attempt them from a written description. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.

title: The Five Voids of the Peacock Feather

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y6 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: śikhipakṣaiś citrarūpair maṇḍalaiḥ śūnyapañcakam | dhyāyato 'nuttare śūnye praveśo hṛdaye bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: For one who meditates on the five voids by way of the many-coloured circles in a peacock's feathers, there is entry into the heart, the unsurpassed void.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the five voids are the five senses (their subtle sources, the tanmātras), seen like the circles of a peacock feather; one meditates in the heart. Singh also notes a double meaning: maṇḍala names both the circles in the feather and the five senses.

instruction: Feel the whole field of the senses as nested rings and let the detail dissolve toward a quiet centre at the heart.

method.text: Optionally look at a peacock feather or a picture of one, then close the eyes. Notice the whole sensory field (sight, sound, touch, taste, smell) as nested rings. Let detail dissolve toward the quiet centre at the heart, without chasing sensation or forcing trance.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 32 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Even, natural breath, about four in and four out. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The five sense-fields (sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell) as rings converging on an empty centre
attention.secondary: The heart as the place of entry named in the verse

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the eye of a peacock feather: rings of colour around an empty centre, used as a picture of the five sense-fields converging on emptiness in the heart.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If attention to the senses becomes overwhelming, open the eyes and look at one simple object in the room. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Attention Dissolving into Space, a Wall, or a Worthy Vessel

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y7 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)
numbering_variants.popular_lists: Old notes say some popular lists put an all-directions space visualisation at dharana 10; that claim could not be traced to a named edition and is unverified.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: īdṛśena krameṇaiva yatra kutrāpi cintanā | śūnye kuḍye pare pātre svayaṃ līnā varapradā ||
dharana.rendering: In the same graded way, wherever attention rests, whether on empty space, on a wall, or on a worthy vessel, it dissolves there by itself and grants the boon.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: 'pare pātre' is read differently: Singh 'some excellent person' (glossed as a pure-minded, competent pupil), Bäumer 'a worthy disciple', Chaudhri 'a great person', Silburn 'receptacle suprême', Wallis 'a perfect vessel'. Singh and S. P. Singh & Maheshvarananda tie 'in this same way' back to the twelve stations of verse 30.

instruction: Rest a soft gaze on empty sky or a blank wall and let attention dissolve into it, blinking whenever needed.

method.text: Rest a soft gaze on empty sky or a blank wall, keep attention there without chasing thoughts, and let it dissolve into the support. Optional variant: briefly rest attention on the presence of someone you hold as worthy, then return to the breath. Contemplative focus only, not ritual or force.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 33 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath, about four in and four out if counting helps. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: One plain support (space, wall, or worthy vessel), held until attention dissolves into it
attention.secondary: Noticing thoughts without following them

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is one line of attention from the practitioner to a single plain support, ending where attention dissolves into it.
points: a single support for attention: empty space, a blank wall, or a worthy vessel

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Blink whenever needed; do not strain the eyes by staring. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.

beats.title: Geometry
beats.script: No shape to make. Sit where you can see open sky or a plain wall. The map is one line of attention to one plain support.

beats.title: Orientation
beats.script: Body supported. Soft, steady gaze on the support. Blink when you need to.

beats.title: Breath
beats.script: Natural breath, four in, four out. No forced hold.

beats.script: Keep attention on the support. Let thoughts pass without following. Let attention melt into what it rests on.

title: Mind Placed Inside the Skull

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y8 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)
numbering_variants.hatha_es: dharana 11 = verse 106 (connection of subject and object); non-standard, not followed (the previous draft of this door followed it)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kapālāntar mano nyasya tiṣṭhan mīlitalocanaḥ | krameṇa manaso dārḍhyāl lakṣayel lakṣyam uttamam ||
dharana.rendering: Remaining with eyes closed, place the mind inside the skull; as steadiness of mind gradually grows, one perceives the highest thing to be perceived.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: 'tiṣṭhan' means remaining or abiding; Singh renders it 'seated', Bäumer 'sitting motionless', Silburn 'se tenant', Wallis 'remaining'. Satsangi locates the attention at the crown of the head and The Mystery Within glosses the place as the sahasrāra cakra; most translators say 'inside the cranium'. Singh also records an esoteric reading of kapāla as the union of Śiva and Śakti.

instruction: Close the eyes and rest attention inside the skull as a soft field, letting steadiness build without force.

method.text: Sit or lie quietly, close the eyes, and place attention inside the skull as a soft field rather than a clenched point. Let mental steadiness build bit by bit without forcing a vision or a blank.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 34 does not prescribe a body position (it specifies closed eyes and uses the verb tiṣṭhan, 'remaining', which Singh renders 'seated'). The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural, even breath, about four in and four out. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The steady space inside the skull, held as a soft field
attention.secondary: Steadiness growing gradually, without forcing a vision or a blank

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the bowl of space inside the skull, held as a soft field rather than a tight point. Closed eyes are part of the verse; posture is not specified.
points: the inner space of the skull (kapāla)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If attention in the head brings pressure or a headache, move attention down to the breath at the belly or open the eyes and stop. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Space Within the Central Channel

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y9 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: madhyanāḍī madhyasaṃsthā bisasūtrābharūpayā | dhyātāntarvyomayā devyā tayā devaḥ prakāśate ||
dharana.rendering: The central channel stands in the middle, slender as the fibre in a lotus stalk; when it is meditated on as the Goddess whose nature is the inner sky, through her the God shines forth.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: meditate on the inner vacuity of the medial channel, which he identifies as the suṣumnā; the verse itself says only 'in the middle'.

instruction: Rest awareness on one slender channel through the middle of the body and feel its inside as open space.

method.text: Rest awareness on one continuous slender channel through the middle of the body, fine as a lotus-stalk fibre, and feel its inside as open space rather than as a muscle to grip. No forcing of breath or effort.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 35 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Equal four-count breath if counting helps, otherwise natural. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: A slender channel through the middle of the body, sensed as open inner space
attention.secondary: The quiet of that inner space

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is one very fine channel running through the middle of the body, felt as open inner space rather than as something to grip.
points: a filament-thin channel through the middle of the body

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If the image brings strong sensations or agitation, open the eyes and feel the whole body resting on the floor. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Sealing the Sense-Doors, Watching the Point Dissolve

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y10 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kararuddhadṛgastreṇa bhrūbhedād dvārarodhanāt | dṛṣṭe bindau kramāl līne tanmadhye paramā sthitiḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Closing the doors [of the senses] with the hands used as a 'weapon' that blocks the eyes, and piercing [the point between] the eyebrows, a point of light (bindu) is seen; as it gradually dissolves, in its midst is the supreme state.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh describes the hand seal: thumbs close the ears, index fingers the eyes, middle fingers the nostrils, ring and little fingers the mouth, so that 'the vital energy is confined within'. Singh also reports that Swami Lakshmanjoo reverses the order: first concentrate on the brow until a drop of light appears, then apply the seal. Because the classical seal covers the eyes and closes the nose and mouth, this door is observe-only.

instruction: Observe only: read the verse and its classical description. This door is not practised.

method.text: Classical method: a seal of the senses with the hands (covering the eyes and the other openings) while piercing attention at the eyebrow centre until an inner point of light appears and fades.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Never press on the eyes or block the nose or mouth. Pressure on the eyeballs and obstruction of breathing are not taught by this school. Skip classical sensory-seal pressure on the eyes in class. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
safety.observe_only_note: Never press on the eyes or block the nose or mouth. Pressure on the eyeballs and obstruction of breathing are not taught by this school. Skip classical sensory-seal pressure on the eyes in class.

title: The Point of Subtle Fire

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y11 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)
numbering_variants.hatha_es: dharana 14 = the text of verse 43 (space in all directions); non-standard, not followed (the previous draft of this door followed it)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: dhāmāntaḥkṣobhasambhūtasūkṣmāgnitilakākṛtim | binduṃ śikhānte hṛdaye layānte dhyāyato layaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: For one who meditates, at the top of the head or in the heart, on the bindu, a tilaka-like spark of subtle fire produced by agitation within the 'abode', there is dissolution at the end of dissolution.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh glosses the 'abode' (dhāma) as the light in the eyes and the agitation as pressure on the eyes. Bäumer has 'by agitating the eye', Chaudhri 'press the eyes gently' and Dubois 'une pression (exercée sur les yeux)' (all as printed in The Mystery Within). Singh also gives an alternative: the sparks seen as a lamp goes out. Wallis renders it more neutrally as 'inner stimulation of the Radiant Abode'.

instruction: Observe only: read the verse and its classical description. This door is not practised.

method.text: Classical method: produce a spark of light by pressure or agitation of the eyes, then meditate on it at the top of the head or in the heart until it dissolves.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Never press or rub the eyes to produce light. This school does not teach eye pressure in any form. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.

title: Bathing in the Unstruck Sound

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y12 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)
numbering_variants.hatha_es: dharana 15 = a variant of verse 42 (piṇḍa-mantra fading into void); non-standard, not followed (the previous draft of this door followed it)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: anāhate pātrakarṇe 'bhagnaśabde sariddrute | śabdabrahmaṇi niṣṇātaḥ paraṃ brahmādhigacchati ||
dharana.rendering: One who is steeped in sound-Brahman, the unstruck (anāhata) and unbroken sound that rushes like a river and is heard by the fit ear, reaches the supreme Brahman.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: niṣṇāta means both 'well-versed' and 'bathed in'; the sound is an inner sound heard by an ear made competent by yoga. Bäumer compares the sound to a waterfall, and Chaudhri adds 'the continuous sound of a river flowing, or by closing the ears' (both as printed in The Mystery Within). The verse itself names neither a waterfall nor closing the ears.

instruction: Listen past ordinary sounds to the subtle, continuous hum of a quiet room and bathe in that unbroken sound.

method.text: Begin with a steady natural sound if helpful (running water, wind, a fan), then let attention move to the subtle continuous hum heard when the room is quiet. Stay immersed in that unbroken sound like bathing in a river. If covering the ears, rest the palms lightly over them without pressing.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 38 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural, quiet breath, about four in and six out if counting helps. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: A steady, unbroken stream of sound, followed from outer to inner
attention.secondary: Being immersed in it rather than analysing it

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a continuous stream of sound flowing through the vessel of the ear, followed inward until the listener is immersed in it.
points: a continuous inner stream of sound

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If listening inward makes a ringing or other sound in the ears feel distressing, stop and listen to ordinary sounds in the room instead. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Praṇava Fading into Void

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: Y13 (Wallis groups verses 24–27 as one technique)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: praṇavādisamuccārāt plutānte śūnyabhāvanāt | śūnyayā parayā śaktyā śūnyatām eti bhairavi ||
dharana.rendering: O Bhairavī, by fully sounding the praṇava (such as Oṃ) and contemplating emptiness at the end of its prolonged (pluta) sound, one reaches emptiness through the supreme power that is emptiness.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer; not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Lakshmanjoo (via the Lakshmanjoo Academy) names three praṇavas, Oṃ, Hūṃ and Hrīṃ, sounded long with attention resting where the sound dissolves. Singh's note gives the same three (Vedic Auṃ, Śaiva Hūṃ, Śākta Hrīṃ) and stresses that at the end of the protracted sound one contemplates the void, not the usual ardhacandra, bindu and other subtle phases.

instruction: Sound a soft, long Oṃ, aloud or silently, and rest in the quiet gap when the sound ends.

method.text: Sound a soft, drawn-out Oṃ (or another seed-syllable you have been taught), or sound it silently. At the moment the sound ends, rest in the quiet gap. Do not chase the next thought. Do not force breath retention or strain to lengthen the sound.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 39 does not prescribe a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Inhale easily. Let the out-breath carry a long, soft Oṃ (or hum it silently) only as long as is comfortable, then rest in the quiet before the next easy in-breath. No forced hold and no straining to make the sound longer.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The moment the sound ends, and the silence after it
attention.secondary: Not reaching for the next thought or the next sound

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is one long sound tapering to nothing, and the open silence after it.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Keep the sound soft and stop before the breath feels short. If you feel light-headed, return to ordinary breathing. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Silence Before and After a Sound

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 40: Syllables emerging from and merging back into silence (Y14 ~ C2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: yasya kasyāpi varṇasya pūrvāntāv anubhāvayet | śūnyayā śūnyabhūto 'sau śūnyākāraḥ pumān bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: Whoever dwells in the silence before any sound-syllable (varṇa) begins and after it ends becomes, through the power of that void, void himself: his very form becomes open space.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: contemplate the condition of a letter before it is uttered and after it is uttered as mere void; 'the power of the void' is parāśakti, and 'becoming the form of the void' means no longer identifying with the breath-body as the Self. Wallis reads 'the beginning and/or ending of any syllable whatsoever'. Singh classes it as śāktopāya ending in śāmbhavopāya.

instruction: Say one soft syllable and rest in the silence just before and just after it.

method.text: Say a single syllable softly, or hear one. Before it, rest in the silence it will come out of; after it, stay in the silence it goes back into. Let the syllable be small and the silences large. No straining to hear.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 40 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. On some out-breaths, say one soft syllable such as 'ma'; let it end with the breath. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The silence immediately before and immediately after a single syllable
attention.secondary: The syllable itself, held lightly

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a line in time: silence, then one syllable, then silence. Attention rests on the two silences that frame the sound.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Keep any voiced syllable soft; there is no need to project the voice. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Following a Long Musical Note to Its End

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 41: Sound of the tambura (Y15 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: tantryādivādyaśabdeṣu dīrgheṣu kramasaṃsthiteḥ | ananyacetāḥ pratyante paravyomavapur bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: One who listens with undivided mind to the long, sustained sounds of stringed and other instruments, following them through their unfolding, becomes at their very end a body of supreme space.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh's notes: a well-produced note seems to come out of eternity and to disappear into it, and when the music stops it still vibrates in memory; if the mind stays with that echo instead of wandering, one is absorbed in the source of all sound (parāvāk). Wallis glosses tantrī as a stringed instrument such as a vīṇā or tambura.

instruction: Listen to one long note until it disappears, and stay in the space it leaves.

method.text: Sound or play one long, sustained note (a string, a bowl, a recorded drone). Listen to it with undivided attention as it unfolds and thins. When it becomes inaudible, do not move on; stay in what remains. Repeat with the next note.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 41 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: One long note: a plucked string, a singing bowl, or a recorded drone, followed to its last trace
attention.secondary: The space that is left when the sound has gone

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the life of one long note: onset, resonance, fading edge, and the space after it. Attention travels with the note and stays at its end.
points: the onset of a sustained note
the edge where it becomes inaudible

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Keep the volume comfortable; do not hold the ear close to a loud instrument. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 42: Mantra-mass (Y16 ~ A3)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: piṇḍamantrasya sarvasya sthūlavarṇakrameṇa tu | ardhendubindunādāntaḥ śūnyoccārād bhavec chivaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: By sounding any piṇḍa-mantra (a compact seed-mantra) through its sequence of audible letters, and then following it through its subtler phases, the half-moon, the point and the resonance, to the end of resonance and into the void, one becomes Śiva.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: uccāra here does not mean mere muttering but moving upward from gross utterance to subtle vibration and finally to mental reflection. A piṇḍamantra is a compact mantra such as AUM or the nine-letter navātma. Singh reports Śivopādhyāya's mapping of AUM onto stations rising from the navel (A) through the heart (U) and mouth (M) to the point between the brows (bindu), the forehead (ardhacandra) and on to unmanā above the head; the audible letters take one measure each, the subtle phases half a measure, unmanā is beyond time.

instruction: Sound Oṃ softly and follow it from voice to hum to silence, resting in the silence.

method.text: Choose a short seed-mantra; this school uses Oṃ. Sound A-U-M audibly on an out-breath, let it become a hum, let the hum become an inner resonance, and let the resonance fade into silence. Rest in the silence before the next round.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 42 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural in-breath. On the out-breath, sound the mantra softly and let it thin out with the breath. Take a free breath between rounds. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The mantra's sequence from audible letters to hum to resonance to silence
attention.secondary: The silence at the end, where the sound has gone

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a mantra growing quieter: audible letters, then the hum, then resonance, then silence. Commentary also pictures these phases rising from the navel to above the head; that is recorded, not required.
points: the hum after the letters (bindu, ardhacandra: commentarial)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Keep the voice soft and the out-breath unforced; take free breaths between rounds. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Space in Every Direction at Once, Within the Body

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 43: Inner space (Y17 ~ C2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: nijadehe sarvadikkaṃ yugapad bhāvayed viyat | nirvikalpamanās tasya viyat sarvam pravartate ||
dharana.rendering: Let one contemplate space (viyat) in every direction at once within one's own body. For one whose mind is free of thought-constructs, everything becomes space.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh stresses two conditions: the contemplation must be simultaneous (yugapat), not direction by direction, and the mind must be still (nirvikalpamanāḥ); then one reaches the plane in which differences fall away. Wallis: 'everything becomes spacious'. Note: a previous House 1 draft of Door 014 carried this verse under hatha.es numbering; under Singh it belongs here.

instruction: Feel space opening in every direction within the body at the same time.

method.text: Feel the body's inner space opening in every direction at once: front, back, sides, up and down together, not one after another. Let thoughts pass without following them, and rest in the openness.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)

seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 43 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: Space in all directions within the body, felt simultaneously
attention.secondary: Thoughts left alone, so the openness can stay simple

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a sphere: the body at its centre and space opening in every direction at the same moment, not one direction after another.
points: space opening in all directions at once

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If the sense of openness feels unsettling, open the eyes and feel the contact of the body with the floor. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Void Above and the Void at the Base

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 44: Space above and below (Y18 ~ A2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: pṛṣṭhaśūnyaṃ mūlaśūnyaṃ yugapad bhāvayec ca yaḥ | śarīranirapekṣiṇyā śaktyā śūnyamanā bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: Whoever contemplates at the same moment the void above and the void at the root becomes, through the power that does not depend on the body, void-minded.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh takes pṛṣṭhaśūnya as 'the void above' and glosses 'the energy independent of the body' as prāṇaśakti; 'void-minded' means free of all thought-constructs. Wallis: the space above, at the crown of the head, and the space at the root of the body. The word pṛṣṭha can also mean 'back'; all three translators consulted read it as 'above'.

instruction: Feel open space above the head and at the base of the body at the same time.

method.text: Feel an open space above the head and an open space at the base of the trunk, both at the same moment. Do not alternate between them. Rest as the mind between them grows empty.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The void above and the void at the base, held simultaneously
attention.secondary: The mind between them becoming quiet

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is two open spaces on the vertical line of the body, one above and one at the base, held at the same moment.

void at the base (commentarial: root of the trunk)

title: Three Voids at Once: Above, Base and Heart

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 45: Three inner voids (Y19 ~ A3)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: pṛṣṭhaśūnyaṃ mūlaśūnyaṃ hṛcchūnyam bhāvayet sthiram | yugapan nirvikalpatvān nirvikalpodayas tataḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Let one steadily contemplate, all at once, the void above, the void at the root and the void in the heart. Because this is free of thought-constructs all at once, the thought-free state arises.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh reports Śivopādhyāya's reading: the void above stands for the knowing subject (pramātṛ), the void at the root for the objects (prameya), and the void in the heart for knowing itself (pramāṇa), each contemplated as void. Wallis: the space above, at the root, and in the heart, simultaneously.

instruction: Feel open space above the head, in the heart and at the base, all at once.

method.text: Feel an open space above the head, in the heart and at the base of the trunk, all three together, and hold that steadily without moving between them. Let the thought-free state come by itself.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)

breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The voids above, in the heart and at the base, held at once and steadily
attention.secondary: The thought-free quiet that follows

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is three open spaces on the vertical line (above, heart, base) held at the same moment and steadily.

title: A Moment of Void in the Body

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 46: Space in any body part (Y20 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: tanūdeśe śūnyataiva kṣaṇamātraṃ vibhāvayet | nirvikalpaṃ nirvikalpo nirvikalpasvarūpabhāk ||
dharana.rendering: If, even for a single moment, one contemplates some region of the body as nothing but void, free of thought-constructs, one becomes thought-free and takes on the nature of the thought-free.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh reads tanūdeśa as the body taken as the limited empirical self and describes three stages: contemplating it without thought-constructs, becoming habitually thought-free, and finally entering the state of Bhairava, whose nature is thought-free. Wallis and Bäumer read tanūdeśa as 'any part (or point) of the body'. This door follows the 'any part of the body' reading and notes Singh's.

instruction: For a moment, sense one part of the body, such as a hand, as empty space.

method.text: Choose one region of the body, such as a hand. For a moment, sense it as nothing but open space, without thinking about it. Let the moment end naturally; repeat a few times.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 46 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

title: The Body's Tissues Pervaded by Space

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 47: Space pervading the tissues (Y21 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: sarvaṃ dehagataṃ dravyaṃ viyadvyāptaṃ mṛgekṣaṇe | vibhāvayet tatas tasya bhāvanā sā sthirā bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: O doe-eyed one, let one contemplate everything that makes up the body (bone, flesh and the rest) as pervaded by space; then that contemplation becomes steady.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: for one who cannot yet contemplate the void directly, this contemplation of the body's constituents (bone, flesh and so on) as pervaded by space steadies the contemplation of vacuity, which finally opens into the light of consciousness. Wallis: 'all the tissues of the body are pervaded by Space'.

instruction: Sense bone, flesh and every tissue of the body as filled through with space.

method.text: Sense the body's tissues one after another (bone, muscle, blood, skin), each as pervaded by space, until the whole body feels porous and open. Rest there.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 47 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.secondary: The steadiness of the contemplation

title: The Skin as a Wall with Nothing Inside

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 48: Wall of skin (Y22 ~ C1)

dharana.rendering: Let one think of the skin of the body as a wall, with nothing at all inside it. Meditating in this way, one comes to share in what cannot be meditated upon.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: everyone habitually identifies with the body; detaching consciousness from its limits develops a sense of all-pervasiveness, and when that is reached there is no longer an object to meditate on, as Bhairava says in verse 16. Wallis: the 'dividing wall' of skin is merely a screen with nothing within.

instruction: Feel the skin as a thin wall and the inside of the body as an empty room.

method.text: Feel the skin all over the body as a thin wall, like the walls of a room. Imagine there is nothing inside it at all. Rest in that emptiness without looking for anything in it.

title: Senses Dissolved in the Space of the Heart

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 49: Lotus in the heart (Y23 ~ A1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: hṛdyākāśe nilīnākṣaḥ padmasampuṭamadhyagaḥ | ananyacetāḥ subhage paraṃ saubhāgyam āpnuyāt ||
dharana.rendering: With the senses dissolved in the space of the heart, entered into the middle of the two bowls of the lotus, with the mind on nothing else, O fortunate one, one gains the highest fortune.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: hṛt is not the physical heart but the central place above the diaphragm, pictured as a lotus of two bowls joined together; following Śivopādhyāya, the upper bowl is knowing, the lower bowl is the known, and the centre is the knower, into which the practitioner plunges. 'Highest fortune' is glossed as supreme bliss (Kṣemarāja cites this verse on Śivasūtra 1.15). Note: the prototype seed doors/049.json used this verse for Door 49; under Singh's numbering it is dharana 26.

instruction: Let the senses settle into the space at the centre of the chest and rest there.

method.text: Let the senses withdraw from their objects and settle into the space at the centre of the chest. Picture it as the middle of a lotus formed by two bowls. Keep the mind there and on nothing else.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 49 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The space at the centre of the chest, between the two bowls of the lotus
attention.secondary: The senses drawn back from their objects

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a small space in the centre of the chest, pictured as the meeting of two bowls, with attention resting in the middle.
points: the space of the heart (commentarial: centre of the chest, not the physical heart)

title: Mind Dissolved at the Dvādaśānta

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 50: Mindfulness of the dvādaśānta (Y24 ~ A2)

dharana.rendering: When the mind dissolves in the dvādaśānta while one's whole body is pervaded (by awareness), the reality that is the goal becomes steadily present for one whose understanding is firm.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh admits it is not clear which bodily dvādaśānta is meant (there are several twelve-finger spans in the body) and suggests the brahmarandhra at the top of the head; Ānandabhaṭṭa's commentary allows the cosmic void or the central channel. Wallis: the dvādaśānta of one's subtle body. Bäumer's version instead reads 'the body is void in all parts'.

instruction: Fill the body with awareness, then let the mind rest and dissolve at the crown.

method.text: Let awareness fill the whole body. Then let the mind rest at a point at the crown or just above it, and let it dissolve there. Keep the understanding steady; return to the point whenever the mind wanders.

attention.secondary: The mind resting and dissolving at the dvādaśānta at or above the crown

title: Returning to the Dvādaśānta Wherever You Are
sanskrit: yathā tathā yatra tatra dvādaśānte manaḥ kṣipet

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 51: Mindfulness of the dvādaśānta, cont’d

dharana.sanskrit_iast: yathā tathā yatra tatra dvādaśānte manaḥ kṣipet | pratikṣaṇaṃ kṣīṇavṛtter vailakṣaṇyaṃ dinair bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: However and wherever one is, let one cast the mind into the dvādaśānta, moment after moment; as the mind's fluctuations wane, within days something extraordinary arises.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the mind may be fixed at any dvādaśānta: above the head, twelve finger-widths outside the nose at the end of the out-breath, or the inner centre. Śivopādhyāya glosses 'extraordinary' as the incomparable state of Bhairava. Wallis's concordance quotes Reps, who renders it 'in worldly activity, keep attentive between the two breaths' and notes it as Lakshmanjoo's favourite.

instruction: During the day, briefly return attention to the space just above the head, again and again.

method.text: During ordinary activity (walking, washing, waiting), briefly place attention at the dvādaśānta: just above the head, or at the end of the out-breath in front of the nose. Then carry on. Do it again and again, a moment at a time.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 51 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The dvādaśānta, returned to briefly and often during the day
attention.secondary: The mind's fluctuation thinning

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is one point returned to again and again through the day, whatever one is doing.
points: the dvādaśānta: above the head, or about twelve finger-widths in front of the nose at the end of the out-breath (commentarial)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Keep your main attention on anything that needs it, such as traffic or tools; this is a light return, not a withdrawal. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
