title: The Fire of Time Rising Through One's Own Body

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 52: Burning the body-image (Y25 ~ A2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kālāgninā kālapadād utthitena svakam puram | pluṣṭam vicintayed ante śāntābhāsas tadā bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: Let one imagine one's own body (the 'city') burnt up by the fire of time (kālāgni) rising from the foot; at the end, one becomes a tranquil radiance.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: one utters a formula (aum ra-kṣa-ra-ya-uṃ tanuṃ dahayāmi namaḥ) and imagines one's body burnt by the flames of Kālāgni Rudra, rising from the toe of the right foot (kālapada); the image is of all the limitations of the body being burnt away, leaving one's essential nature, all peace. Wallis: 'one's own body (/fortress) is incinerated by the Fire of Time rising from the feet'.

instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class. For practice, use Door 024 or Door 025.

method.text: Classical method: while uttering a formula, one visualises the fire of time rising from the toe of the right foot and burning one's whole body, and at the end rests in a tranquil radiance.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Not led as a practice: visualising one's own body burning can be distressing. Anyone with trauma, self-harm history or strong anxiety should skip this imagery entirely. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
safety.observe_only_note: Observe-only. Imagery of one's own body burning can be distressing, especially for anyone with trauma or self-harm history; this school does not lead it. Read it as a description of letting limitation go. For practice, use a gentle space door such as Door 024 or Door 025.

title: The Whole World Burnt by the Fire of Time

dharana.sanskrit_iast: evam eva jagat sarvaṃ dagdhaṃ dhyātvā vikalpataḥ | ananyacetasaḥ puṃsaḥ pumbhāvaḥ paramo bhavet ||

title: Principles Dissolving into Their Sources

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 54: Purifying the elements (Y27 ~ A2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: svadehe jagato vāpi sūkṣmasūkṣmatarāṇi ca | tattvāni yāni nilayaṃ dhyātvānte vyajyate parā ||
dharana.rendering: If one meditates on the principles (tattvas) of one's own body, or of the world, subtle and ever subtler, as dissolving each into its source, then at the end the supreme Goddess (parā) is revealed.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the technique of fusion (vyāpti): the gross elements are contemplated as absorbed into the subtle elements, these into the ego-principle, that into intellect, that into prakṛti and so on until all is reabsorbed in Sadāśiva; then parā devī is revealed and everything appears as her expression. Singh calls this ātmavyāpti and notes a further stage, śivavyāpti, in verse 57 (Door 034).

instruction: Let solidity dissolve into fluidity, fluidity into warmth, warmth into movement, movement into space, and space into awareness.

method.text: Feel the body's solidity and let it dissolve into fluidity; fluidity into warmth; warmth into movement; movement into space; space into awareness. Rest in what remains. (The full classical series of principles is longer; this is a school simplification.)

attention.secondary: What remains when the layers are folded back

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a nested series, each layer dissolving into the subtler one that contains it, ending in open awareness.

title: Thick Breath, Thin Breath, Entering the Heart

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 55: Freedom in the dream state (Y28 ~ A3)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: pīnāṃ ca durbalāṃ śaktiṃ dhyātvā dvādaśagocare | praviśya hṛdaye dhyāyan muktaḥ svātantryam āpnuyāt ||
dharana.rendering: Having meditated on the breath-power as thick and as thin in the region of the dvādaśānta, and entering the heart while meditating, one becomes free and gains sovereign freedom. (In the reading of Abhinavagupta and Kṣemarāja: one gains freedom in dream.)
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh translates: gross prāṇaśakti made frail and subtle by yogic discipline (particularly prāṇāyāma) and meditated on in the dvādaśānta or the heart. He then gives Swami Lakshmanjoo's traditional reading: 'thick' means breathing in and out audibly, 'thin' means slowly; meditating so at the dvādaśānta and the heart while falling asleep, one gains freedom in dreams. Singh records that Abhinavagupta (Tantrāloka 15) reads suptaḥ svācchandyam āpnuyāt and Kṣemarāja (Spandanirṇaya) svapnasvātantryam āpnuyāt. Wallis: prāṇa thick in the heart, tenuous at the dvādaśānta, and 'freedom in one's dreams'.

instruction: Breathe a few soft audible breaths, let the breath grow thin, and rest attention in the heart.

method.text: Breathe a few soft, audible breaths with attention at the dvādaśānta. Let the breath become thin and slow by itself. Then let attention enter the heart and rest there; in the traditional reading, while falling asleep. No breath-holding and no forceful breathing.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position. In Lakshmanjoo's reading the practice is done while falling asleep, so lying down is natural.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 55 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: A few soft, audible breaths, then let the breath become thin and slow on its own. Never strain or hold. Natural breath is always fine.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The breath-power at the dvādaśānta and in the heart, first coarse, then fine
attention.secondary: Entering the heart as the breath thins

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the breath travelling between two places, the dvādaśānta and the heart, sometimes full and audible, sometimes thin and slow.

title: The Paths of Manifestation Dissolving Step by Step

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 56: The system of paths (Y29 ~ A3)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: bhuvanādhvādirūpeṇa cintayet kramaśo 'khilam | sthūlasūkṣmaparasthityā yāvad ante manolayaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Let one contemplate the whole of reality, step by step, in the form of the 'paths' (adhvan), beginning with the path of worlds, as resolving from gross into subtle and from subtle into supreme, until at the end the mind dissolves.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh explains the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) of Trika: on the side of word, phoneme (varṇa), mantra and word (pada); on the side of object, aspect (kalā), principle (tattva) and world (bhuvana). The practice is to imagine the gross pair (pada, bhuvana) dissolving into the subtle pair (mantra, tattva), that into the supreme pair (varṇa, kalā), and finally all into pure consciousness, step by step (kramaśaḥ), so that the individual mind dissolves. Singh contrasts it with verse 54 (Door 031), which leads only as far as the revealed Goddess.

instruction: Let the solid world and your words resolve, step by step, into subtler levels and finally into awareness.

method.text: Contemplate the world around you and the words you think in as the gross level. Let them resolve into subtler patterns (principles, the shapes of sound), those into their creative source, and that into pure awareness. Take each step only when the previous one feels clear. Rest when the mind dissolves.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The world and its words, contemplated as resolving gross into subtle into supreme
attention.secondary: The mind itself dissolving at the end

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is three levels folding back one into the next, gross into subtle into supreme, ending in pure consciousness.

title: The Whole Universe Seen as Śiva, All at Once

instruction: Contemplate the whole universe as empty and let the mind rest in that emptiness.

instruction: Look into the hollow of a bowl or jar, ignore its walls, and rest in the space inside.

title: Gazing over Open Country

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 60: Gazing on an open field (Y32 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: nirvṛkṣagiribhittyādideśe dṛṣṭiṃ vinikṣipet | vilīne mānase bhāve vṛttikṣīṇaḥ prajāyate ||
dharana.rendering: Let one cast the gaze over a place free of trees, hills, walls and the like. As the mental state dissolves there, the fluctuations of the mind cease.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: when the mind rests on a vast vacant space without the support of any definite object, its thought-constructs stop, and the light within makes itself felt. Abhinavagupta quotes the first line in his Parātrīśikā commentary as an entry into Bhairava-consciousness. Singh calls the fixed gaze into open space dṛṣṭibandhana-bhāvanā and classes it as śāmbhavopāya.

instruction: Rest your gaze on a wide, empty view and let the mind go quiet with it.

method.text: Find a wide, open view (open land, water, sky) without trees, hills or buildings in the foreground. Let the gaze rest on the openness without picking any object. Let the mind go quiet with it. Blink normally.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position facing an open view: a field, a beach, a wide sky, or a large empty wall if nothing else is available.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 60 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: A wide, empty expanse with nothing for the eye to hold
attention.secondary: The mind's fluctuations falling quiet

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a wide, empty view: open land, water or sky with nothing for the eye to hold on to.
points: a wide, open expanse with no objects to catch the eye

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Never look at the sun. Blink freely; this is a soft, wide gaze, not a stare. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Middle Between Two Perceptions
sanskrit: ubhayor bhāvayor jñāne dhyātvā madhyaṃ samāśrayet

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 61: Noticing the space between (Y33 ~ C2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: ubhayor bhāvayor jñāne dhyātvā madhyaṃ samāśrayet | yugapac ca dvayaṃ tyaktvā madhye tattvam prakāśate ||
dharana.rendering: At the moment of knowing two things, let one rest in the middle between them. Letting go of both at once, reality shines in the middle.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: when the mind holds two perceptions or ideas, drop both together and settle in the gap between them; reality flashes forth there. The two are not pushed aside by effort but released by gentle non-observation (anālocana). Singh calls it a very important and unfailing dhāraṇā, notes it is quoted in the Netra Tantra as contemplation without support, and records Jayaratha's reading jñātvā ('having known') for dhyātvā ('having meditated').

instruction: Notice two things, let both go at once, and rest in the space between them.

method.text: Notice two things, for example two sounds, two sensations, or two thoughts. Rather than holding either, let both go together and rest in the space between them. Release them gently, not by pushing.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 61 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The gap between two perceptions or thoughts
attention.secondary: Releasing both at once, gently

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is two points with a gap between them; attention rests in the gap and lets both points go.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Keep it gentle; there is nothing to suppress. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Not Moving On to the Next Thing
sanskrit: bhāve tyakte niruddhā cin naiva bhāvāntaraṃ vrajet

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 62: Centering in the space between (Y34 ~ C2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: bhāve tyakte niruddhā cin naiva bhāvāntaraṃ vrajet | tadā tanmadhyabhāvena vikasatyati bhāvanā ||
dharana.rendering: When one object of mind has been let go and awareness, restrained, does not move on to another, then through that in-between state contemplation blossoms intensely.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: verse 61 drops two positive perceptions; here the gap is between one object released and another that is not allowed to arise. Abhinavagupta refers to both (Tantrāloka 1.84, with Jayaratha's commentary). Singh notes that the Kashmir Series text reads bhāve nyakte ('fixed on an object never seen before') and argues that bhāve tyakte ('when an object is let go'), followed here, is the better reading.

instruction: When a thought ends, don't reach for the next one; stay in the space it leaves.

method.text: Let one thought or perception end. Before reaching for the next, pause and stay in the space that is left. Do not suppress what comes; simply do not move on to it yet.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 62 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The moment after one thought or perception ends, before the next is taken up
attention.secondary: The opening of that in-between state

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is one point that has just been let go and an empty space where the next one would have come.
points: the next object, not taken up

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. This is not forced blankness; if strain appears, let thoughts come and go freely. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Body and World as Consciousness, All at Once
sanskrit: sarvaṃ dehaṃ cinmayaṃ hi jagad vā

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 63: The body-world is awareness (Y35 ~ B2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: sarvaṃ dehaṃ cinmayaṃ hi jagad vā paribhāvayet | yugapan nirvikalpena manasā paramodayaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Let one contemplate the whole body, or the world, as made of consciousness, all at once and with a mind free of thought-constructs; then comes the supreme awakening.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh stresses two conditions: an unwavering mind free of doubts and alternatives (nirvikalpena manasā), and simultaneity (yugapat), in one sweep, not piece by piece. The supreme awakening is the recognition that the whole universe is enveloped in divine light.

instruction: Take in your whole body, then the world, in one sweep, as made of awareness.

method.text: Take in the whole body in one sweep, not part by part, as made of awareness. If that is clear, widen to the whole world. Hold it with a steady, unhesitating mind.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 63 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The whole body or world contemplated as consciousness, all at once
attention.secondary: An unwavering mind, not second-guessing

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the whole body, or the whole world, taken in one sweep as made of awareness.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If one sweep is not possible, start with a small region and widen slowly. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Meeting of the Two Breaths

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 64: Fusion of inhalation and exhalation (Y36 ~ A3)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: vāyudvayasya saṃghaṭṭād antar vā bahir antataḥ | yogī samatvavijñānasamudgamanabhājanam ||
dharana.rendering: From the meeting (saṃghaṭṭa) of the two breaths, within or outside, at its culmination the yogī becomes a vessel for the dawning of the knowledge of sameness (samatva).
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: by the fusion of prāṇa and apāna, at the centre or at the dvādaśānta, there finally arises a complete cessation of both; meditating on that void, in which neither breath is felt, the experience of equality arises. Wallis renders saṃghaṭṭa as 'dynamic tension' and rates the technique advanced.

title: Body and World Filled with One's Own Bliss

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 65: Body of bliss (Y37 ~ A2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: sarvaṃ jagat svadehaṃ vā svānandabharitaṃ smaret | yugapat svāmṛtenaiva parānandamayo bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: Let one call to mind the whole world, or one's own body, as filled with one's own bliss, all at once; through that inner nectar one becomes full of supreme bliss.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: 'all at once' means with the totality of attention in one sweep; 'one's own bliss' is the bliss of consciousness, not pleasure from objects; 'nectar' signals that it does not change. Kṣemarāja cites the verse on Śivasūtra 1.18 and 3.39. Singh reports Lakshmanjoo's reading of vā as 'and': the world and the body together.

instruction: Let a quiet, inner gladness fill your whole body, then the world around you.

method.text: Recall a simple, quiet gladness that does not depend on anything outside. Let it fill the whole body at once, then the world around. Rest in that fullness without chasing intensity.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 65 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The body, or body and world, felt as filled with one's own quiet joy
attention.secondary: That joy as inner, not dependent on anything outside

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the body, or the body and the world, filled evenly with a quiet, inner gladness.
points: both filled with one's own quiet joy

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If no gladness is available today, that is fine; rest with whatever is present without forcing a feeling. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Sudden Joy from a Trick or a Wonder

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 66: Trick-method (Y38 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kuhanena prayogeṇa sadya eva mṛgekṣaṇe | samudeti mahānando yena tattvaṃ prakāśate ||
dharana.rendering: O doe-eyed one, by the use of a trick (kuhana), great joy arises at once, and through it reality is revealed.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh reads kuhana as a magical performance: the spectator's ordinary mind is lifted into mute wonder and joy, free of thought-constructs, and in that moment the nature of Bhairava is revealed; any awe-inspiring scene works the same way. Singh also reports Lakshmanjoo's reading of kuhana as tickling (the armpit), contemplating the essence of the joy that arises. Wallis: 'a trick'; Śivopādhyāya (as cited by Wallis) glosses the reality revealed as the thought-free state.

instruction: When something astonishes you, notice the instant thought stops and rest in it.

method.text: When something astonishes you (a magic trick, a sudden beautiful sight, an unexpected laugh), notice the instant when thinking stops and joy rises. Turn attention to that instant itself and rest in it as long as it lasts.

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 67: Formication (Y39 ~ A3)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: sarvasrotonibandhena prāṇaśaktyordhvayā śanaiḥ | pipīlasparśavelāyām prathate paramaṃ sukham ||

title: Between Fire and Poison

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 68: Mindful sex: between fire and poison (Y40 ~ A3)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: vahner viṣasya madhye tu cittaṃ sukhamayaṃ kṣipet | kevalaṃ vāyupūrṇaṃ vā smarānandena yujyate ||
dharana.rendering: Let one cast the mind, full of pleasure, into the middle between 'fire' (vahni) and 'poison' (viṣa), either on its own or filled with breath; one is then joined with the bliss of love (smarānanda).
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh explains vahni and viṣa as technical terms: vahni is contraction (the descending kuṇḍalinī), viṣa (from viṣ, 'to pervade', not 'poison') is expansion (the rising kuṇḍalinī); 'filled with breath' means the breath restrained so that it leaves through no opening, and the joy of sexual union is here an inner union. Wallis titles it 'Mindful sex: between fire and poison' and reads it as attention between the start and end of sexual union, with forms of breath retention (kevala- or pūraka-kumbhaka).

instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class.

method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

title: The Delight at the Culmination of Union

dharana.rendering: The delight that comes at the culmination of union with a partner (śakti), when one is absorbed in her through that excitement, is the delight of brahman; that delight is said to be one's own.

Wallis reads śakti as a consecrated female partner.

title: Merging with a Great Joy, Such as Meeting a Friend

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 71: The Joy of Meeting Friends (Y43 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: ānande mahati prāpte dṛṣṭe vā bāndhave cirāt | ānandam udgataṃ dhyātvā tallayas tanmanā bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: When a great joy is attained, or on seeing a friend or relative after a long time, let one meditate on the joy that has arisen; absorbed in it, the mind becomes one with it.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: on such occasions one should lay hold of the source of the experience, the pure spiritual pulse (spanda), and meditate on it until the mind is steeped in it; because the experience vanishes quickly it should be seized as soon as it occurs. Wallis: meditate on that joy as it slowly disappears; let the mind dissolve into it.

instruction: When great joy arrives, turn from its cause to the joy itself and merge with it.

method.text: When a great joy arrives (seeing a friend after a long time, good news), turn attention from the event to the joy itself. Feel it as it rises, stay with it, and let the mind merge with it, also as it fades. Do it at once; such moments pass quickly.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 71 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The joy itself as it arises, rather than its cause
attention.secondary: Staying with it as it fades

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a wave of joy in time: it rises with an occasion, and attention turns from the occasion to the joy itself.
points: the joy itself, attended to directly

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Stay present with the person in front of you; this is a quiet inner turning, not a withdrawal from them. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: if one meditates on the full condition of the joy that comes even from satisfying bodily needs, one finds that its source is the divine pulse (spanda), and absorbed in it one experiences spiritual bliss. attention.secondary: The state of fullness itself, beyond the particular taste

title: Resting the Mind Wherever It Is Content
sanskrit: yatra yatra manas tuṣṭir manas tatraiva dhārayet

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 74: Wherever the heart-mind finds delight (Y46 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: yatra yatra manas tuṣṭir manas tatraiva dhārayet | tatra tatra parānandasvarūpaṃ sampravartate ||
dharana.rendering: Wherever the mind finds contentment, let it be held right there; in each such place the very nature of supreme bliss shows itself.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: tuṣṭi means a deep, moving delight, not agitation: one in which everything external is forgotten, thought-constructs fall away and the mind is unruffled. One should plunge into the source of that delight and find it to be the divine, the Self of all.

instruction: Whenever you notice the mind is quietly content, stay right there and rest in it.

method.text: During the day, notice when the mind is quietly content (a cup of tea, a view, a task going well). Instead of moving on, hold the mind right there and rest in the contentment itself.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.

attention.primary: Any moment of quiet contentment, held without reaching for more
attention.secondary: The source of that contentment

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map can be anywhere: whatever place or moment in the day brings quiet contentment, attention settles there.
points: any place, activity or object where the mind is quietly content

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Choose quiet, harmless contentment, not agitation or compulsion. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Threshold of Sleep

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 75: On the edge of sleep (Y47 ~ A1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: anāgatāyāṃ nidrāyām praṇaṣṭe bāhyagocare | sāvasthā manasā gamyā parā devī prakāśate ||
dharana.rendering: When sleep has not yet come but the outer world has faded away, that state can be reached by the mind; there the supreme Goddess shines.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the in-between state of sleep and waking is a thought-free (nirvikalpa) state, which he identifies with the fourth (turīya), transcendental state; concentrating on it one experiences the nature of the Self, called here parā devī. Wallis: 'on the edge of sleep'.

instruction: As you fall asleep, notice the quiet edge just before sleep and rest there.

method.text: Lie down as for sleep. As the outer world fades, notice the quiet state just before sleep arrives. Rest attention lightly on that edge. If you fall asleep, that is fine.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Lying down as for sleep, which is where this threshold naturally occurs.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 75 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The threshold where the outer world has faded and sleep has not yet come
attention.secondary: Its clarity and quiet

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a threshold in time: the outer world has faded, sleep has not yet come, and attention rests on the edge.
points: waking, with the outer world fading

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Let sleep come if it comes; do not keep yourself awake on purpose. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Gazing at Space Dappled with Light

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 76: Patterns of light (Y48 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: tejasā sūryadīpāder ākāśe śabalīkṛte | dṛṣṭir niveśyā tatraiva svātmarūpam prakāśate ||
dharana.rendering: Let the gaze be placed on space made many-coloured by the light of the sun, a lamp and the like; right there one's own nature shines.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: 'and the like' includes the moon, whose light dapples the night sky; in such contemplation the yogī casts off the limitation of objective consciousness and experiences the infinity of consciousness. Wallis: a space 'dappled with the light of the sun or a lamp'.

instruction: Rest a soft gaze on a space patterned with light, without naming anything.

method.text: Find a space patterned by light, such as sunlight through leaves, lamplight on a wall, or moonlight. Rest the gaze softly in the play of light without naming anything. Blink normally.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 76 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: A space patterned with light: sunlight through leaves, lamplight, moonlight
attention.secondary: Seeing itself, rather than the objects

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a patch of space patterned by light, where the gaze rests without picking out objects.
points: a patch of space lit and patterned by light (sunlight through leaves, lamplight, moonlight)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Never look at the sun or any bright light source directly; look at the light where it falls. Blink freely. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Five Seals at the Moment of Seeing

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 77: Krama mudrās (Y49-53; B2, A2, C2, A2 & A4 respectively)
numbering_variants.wallis_grouping: Wallis counts the five mudrās of verse 77 as five yuktis (Y49–53).

dharana.sanskrit_iast: karaṅkiṇyā krodhanayā bhairavyā lelihānayā | khecaryā dṛṣṭikāle ca parāvāptiḥ prakāśate ||
dharana.rendering: Through the seals (mudrā) called karaṅkiṇī, krodhanā, bhairavī, lelihānā and khecarī, at the moment of seeing, the supreme attainment shines forth.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh, following Lakshmanjoo, takes dṛṣṭikāla as 'at the time of practice' and describes each mudrā: karaṅkiṇī views the world as a mere skeleton and the body as dissolved in the highest space; krodhanā is a tense, tight disposition; bhairavī keeps the eyes fixed outward without blinking while attention turns inward; lelihānā 'tastes' the universe as one's own I-consciousness; khecarī has several forms, including turning the tongue back toward the palate, and in its highest form is remaining in Śiva-consciousness. Wallis notes that the Sanskrit commentaries are needed to understand the verse and counts the five mudrās as five yuktis (Y49–53).

instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class. For a gentle gaze practice, use Door 057 or Door 061.

method.text: Classical method: five seals (karaṅkiṇī, krodhanā, bhairavī, lelihānā, khecarī), each described only in commentary, are practised at the moment of perception, and the supreme attainment shines forth.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. The physical forms of these seals (tongue-turning, sustained unblinking gaze, tense holding) are not taught by this school. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
safety.observe_only_note: Observe-only. These seals are esoteric and commentary-dependent, and some forms (tongue-turning, sustained unblinking gaze, tense holding) can strain the body. For a gentle gaze practice, use Door 057 or Door 061.

title: The Space in the Armpits

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 79: Space in the armpits (Y55 ~ A1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: upaviśyāsane samyag bāhū kṛtvārdhakuñcitau | kakṣavyomni manaḥ kurvañ śamam āyāti tallayāt ||
dharana.rendering: Seated properly on a seat, with the arms half-bent, let one place the mind in the space of the armpits; absorbed in that, one comes to peace.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh translates the arms as 'in the form of an arch overhead' and the gaze as fixed in the armpits, and says the arrangement is meant to put the mind at ease. Wallis and Bäumer read only 'half-bending the arms' and 'the space (void) of the armpits'. This door follows the verse's own wording (arms half-bent) and records Singh's reading.

instruction: Sit with the arms half-bent and rest attention in the space under each arm.

method.text: Sit comfortably. Let the arms rest half-bent, for example with the hands resting on the thighs, so there is a little space under each arm. Place the mind in that space and let it settle there. Lower or rest the arms whenever they tire.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition, with one exception that belongs to the verse: verse 79 itself says to sit properly with the arms half-bent; that arm position belongs to the verse, not to the school. That position is recorded in the method as part of the classical description, without any posture name. Everything else about the seat is a convenience, not part of the technique.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The space under each arm
attention.secondary: The peace that comes as the mind settles there

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is two small hollows of space, one under each arm, where the mind rests. The half-bent arms only make room for them.
points: the space under the left arm
the space under the right arm

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If the arms or shoulders tire, rest the hands on the thighs or lower the arms completely; there is no position to hold. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: A Steady Gaze on a Solid Object

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 80: Looking without a story (Y56 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: sthūlarūpasya bhāvasya stabdhāṃ dṛṣṭiṃ nipātya ca | acireṇa nirādhāraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā śivaṃ vrajet ||
dharana.rendering: Having let a steady, unmoving gaze fall on some solid, physical thing, and soon making the mind free of support, one goes to Śiva.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: fix the gaze without blinking on a gross object while directing attention inward; 'without support' means free of thought-constructs, which are the mind's props. Singh identifies this as the bhairavī mudrā and classes it as śāmbhavopāya. Wallis: 'making the mind free of thoughts and projections about that being'.

instruction: Rest a steady gaze on one simple object and let go of all thoughts about it.

method.text: Place a simple object in front of you. Let the gaze rest on it steadily. Let go of names, judgments and stories about it, so the mind has nothing to lean on. Blink whenever the eyes need to.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 80 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: One simple object, seen steadily
attention.secondary: The mind letting go of thoughts about it

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a straight line of gaze from the eyes to one simple object, with the mind letting go of everything it thinks about that object.
points: a simple physical object (a stone, a cup, a candle-holder)

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Blink whenever needed: the classical gaze is unblinking, but this school does not ask for it. Stop if the eyes water or strain. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Mouth Open, Mentally Sounding 'Ha'

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 81: Mental uccāra of ‘ha’ (Y57 ~ A1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: madhyajihve sphāritāsye madhye nikṣipya cetanām | hoccāraṃ manasā kurvaṃs tataḥ śānte pralīyate ||
dharana.rendering: With the mouth wide open and the tongue in the middle, placing awareness in the middle, and sounding 'ha' in the mind, one dissolves into peace.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh reads the tongue as inverted against the palate (khecarī mudrā, as described in the Vivekamārtaṇḍa) and explains: the breath naturally sounds haṃsa; with the tongue inverted the 's' cannot form and only 'ha' remains, a vowel-less 'ha' that can only be sounded mentally, and repeating it develops the middle state. Wallis and Bäumer read 'the tongue in the middle of the wide open mouth'; Wallis adds 'pointing up'. This door follows the plain reading and does not teach tongue inversion.

instruction: Let the mouth fall open, rest the tongue in the middle, and silently sound 'ha'.

method.text: Let the jaw relax so the mouth opens wide, without strain. Rest the tongue in the middle of the mouth. Place awareness in the middle of that open space and sound 'ha' silently, in the mind only. Let it dissolve into peace.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 81 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath through the nose or the open mouth, whichever is comfortable. The 'ha' is silent, in the mind only. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The middle of the open mouth
attention.secondary: The silent, mental 'ha'

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the open space of the mouth, the tongue resting in its middle, and a silent 'ha' sounding in that space.
points: the tongue resting in the middle
the mental sound 'ha' in the middle of the open space

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Open the mouth only as wide as is comfortable; close it whenever the jaw tires. Tongue inversion is not taught. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Body Contemplated as Unsupported

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 82: Floating without support (Y58 ~ A2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: āsane śayane sthitvā nirādhāraṃ vibhāvayan | svadehaṃ manasi kṣīṇe kṣaṇāt kṣīṇāśayo bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: Resting on a seat or a bed, let one contemplate one's own body as without support; as the mind fades, in an instant one becomes free of one's stored dispositions.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: though actually resting on a seat or bed, one contemplates with firm conviction that the body has no support at all; the mind becomes free of the thought-constructs that serve as its props, and with that the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) lying in the unconscious also vanish. Wallis: 'floating without support'.

instruction: Resting on a seat or bed, feel your body as if nothing were holding it up.

method.text: Sit on a seat or lie on a bed, fully supported. Then contemplate the body as having no support at all, as if floating in open space. Let the mind quieten as it loses its props.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Sitting on a seat or lying on a bed, as the verse says; fully supported in fact.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 82 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The body felt as unsupported, floating
attention.secondary: The mind growing quiet as it loses its props

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the body pictured floating, with nothing beneath it, while in fact it rests on a seat or bed.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If the floating image brings unease or a falling feeling, feel the support again and open the eyes. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Gentle Rocking or Swaying

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 83: Rocking the body (Y59 ~ A1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: calāsane sthitasyātha śanair vā dehacālanāt | praśānte mānase bhāve devi divyaugham āpnuyāt ||
dharana.rendering: For one seated on a moving seat, or through slowly rocking the body, as the mind becomes calm, O Goddess, one attains the divine flood.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: seated in a cart, on horseback or on any moving vehicle, the body sways to and fro, or one may sway it oneself; a peculiar joy arises, the mind turns inward and grows calm. He explains divyaugha as the 'divine stream' of wisdom, one of three streams (human, perfected, divine). Wallis: a swing or moving seat, or slow rocking of the body.

instruction: Rock slowly and gently, or sit on a moving seat, and rest in the calm it brings.

method.text: Sit on a gently moving seat (a swing, a rocking chair, a passenger seat), or sit still and sway the body slowly and softly to and fro. Let the rhythm calm the mind and rest in that calm.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: A seat that moves gently (a swing, a rocking chair, a passenger seat in a vehicle), or any steady seat in which the body can sway slowly.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 83 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The slow rocking movement and the calm that grows within it
attention.secondary: The mind turning inward

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a gentle pendulum: the body rocking slowly to and fro, and the stillness that appears in the mind within the movement.
points: the moving seat or the slowly swaying body
the calm centre of the movement

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Only as a passenger, never while driving. Keep the movement slow and small; stop if dizzy or queasy. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.

title: Gazing into a Clear Sky

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 84: Sky-gazing (Y60 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: ākāśaṃ vimalam paśyan kṛtvā dṛṣṭiṃ nirantarām | stabdhātmā tatkṣaṇād devi bhairavaṃ vapur āpnuyāt ||
dharana.rendering: Looking at the clear sky with an uninterrupted gaze, becoming utterly still, in that very instant, O Goddess, one attains the form of Bhairava.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: becoming still means the sense of the body vanishes and thoughts and emotions are arrested; the vastness of the sky lets the viewer be lost in a sense of infinity; 'fixed eyes' means without blinking. Singh classes it as śāmbhavopāya. Wallis: 'sky-gazing'.

instruction: Rest a steady gaze in a clear sky, away from the sun, and become still.

method.text: Lie or sit where you can see a clear sky, well away from the sun. Let the gaze rest in it steadily and become still. Let the vastness take attention. Blink whenever needed.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position with a clear view of open sky; lying on the back outdoors works well.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 84 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: A clear, cloudless sky, seen without interruption
attention.secondary: The stillness that comes with it

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a clear sky filling the field of view, with nothing for the eye to hold on to.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Never look at or near the sun. Blink whenever needed: the classical gaze is unblinking, but this school does not ask for it. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Whole Sky Dissolved in the Head

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 85: The sky is in your head (Y61 ~ C2)

dharana.rendering: Let one contemplate all of space, as Bhairava himself, dissolved in one's head; then one enters all of it as the luminous reality of Bhairava's form.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: by creative contemplation (bhāvanā) one imagines the vast sky as Bhairava's expression, dissolved in the space inside the head; that inner space becomes a symbol of Bhairava's infinity and the whole universe is felt bathed in his light. Wallis: 'the sky is in your head', so that the head is continuous with the sky.

instruction: Picture the whole sky gathered into the space inside your head, until they are one.

method.text: Picture the whole sky. Let it gather into the space inside your head, until the inside of the head and the sky feel like one continuous, luminous space. Rest there.

seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 85 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The whole sky felt as dissolved in the space inside the head
attention.secondary: Everything bathed in that light

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the whole sky drawn into the space inside the head until the two are one continuous space.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Keep it light and spacious; if pressure in the head appears, let the image go and feel the feet. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.

title: Waking, Dream and Deep Sleep as One Light

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 86: The three states (Y62 ~ B2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kiñcij jñātaṃ dvaitadāyi bāhyālokas tamaḥ punaḥ | viśvādi bhairavaṃ rūpaṃ jñātvānantaprakāśabhṛt ||
dharana.rendering: Waking, with its partial knowing that brings duality; dream, with its outer appearances; and deep sleep, which is darkness: knowing these states, beginning with waking (viśva), as Bhairava's own form, one comes to hold the infinite light.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.

Wallis and Bäumer read the three phrases in the same way.

instruction: Contemplate waking, dreaming and deep sleep as one awareness passing through three states.

attention.secondary: The light that is present in all three

title: Darkness Before Closed Eyes, Then Before Open Eyes

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 88: Darkness with eyes closed (Y64 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: evam eva nimīlyādau netre kṛṣṇābham agrataḥ | prasārya bhairavaṃ rūpam bhāvayaṃs tanmayo bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: In the same way, first closing the eyes and contemplating the darkness in front, then opening them and extending that dark form of Bhairava outward, one becomes one with it.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: even outside the dark fortnight, one first contemplates the darkness in front with closed eyes, then, with eyes wide open, contemplates the dark form of Bhairava in front; the verse marks the passage from absorption with closed eyes (nimīlana samādhi) to absorption with open eyes (unmīlana samādhi). Wallis: 'darkness with eyes closed'.

instruction: Rest in the darkness behind closed eyes, then open the eyes and feel that same darkness spread out in front.

method.text: Close the eyes and rest attention in the darkness in front of them. When that is steady, open the eyes slowly and feel the same darkness extended outward in front of you, as one field. Rest in it.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The darkness in front of the closed eyes
attention.secondary: The same darkness, felt in front of the open eyes

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the dark field in front of the eyes, first with the eyes closed, then carried outward when they open.
points: the darkness in front of the closed eyes

title: When a Sense Is Blocked, the Void Behind It

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 89: Sensory deprivation (Y65 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: yasya kasyendriyasyāpi vyāghātāc ca nirodhataḥ | praviṣṭasyādvaye śūnye tatraivātmā prakāśate ||
dharana.rendering: When any sense, whichever it is, is obstructed (by something striking it from outside) or deliberately blocked, one enters the non-dual void, and right there the Self shines.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: when a sense is obstructed by an external cause, naturally, or by a self-imposed device, it cannot contact the world, a feeling of emptiness arises in it, the mind turns inward and is absorbed in a void without subject-object duality, where the Self is revealed. Bäumer reads vyāghāta as obstruction 'by striking (an external object)'.

instruction: Gently block one sense, such as covering the ears, and rest in the empty space that opens.

method.text: Gently block one sense: rest the palms lightly over the ears, or use earplugs, or simply close the eyes. Notice the emptiness that appears where the sense was reaching out, and rest in that space. Also notice such moments when they happen by themselves, such as a sudden silence.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 89 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The empty space that appears when one sense is gently blocked
attention.secondary: The Self shining there

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is one sense going quiet, and the empty, inward space that appears where it used to reach outward.
points: the gentle block (palms over the ears)
the empty space where the sense had been reaching out

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Use only gentle blocks: palms resting lightly on the ears, earplugs, or closed eyes. Never press on the eyes or ears, and never block the nose or mouth. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Sounding the Plain Letter 'A'

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 90: The phoneme ‘a’ (Y66 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: abindum avisargaṃ ca akāraṃ japato mahān | udeti devi sahasā jñānaughaḥ parameśvaraḥ ||
dharana.rendering: For one who repeats the letter 'a' without the nasal dot (bindu) and without the out-breathed 'ḥ' (visarga), O Goddess, a great flood of knowledge, the Supreme Lord, rises suddenly.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: 'a' with bindu would be 'aṃ' (an in-breath) and with visarga 'aḥ' (an out-breath); without either, it implies sounding 'a' in a state of breath retention, according to the commentary. Lakshmanjoo instead reads the commentary's 'retention' as a posture of the mouth (cakita mudrā: mouth wide open, tongue drawn back), so that 'a' can only be sounded mentally. 'A' is chosen as the first letter, source of all others, the symbol of the absolute (anuttara) and of perfect I-consciousness (aham).

instruction: Repeat a soft, plain 'a' sound, aloud or silently, with no hum and no breathy ending.

method.text: Sound a soft, plain 'a' (as in 'father'), without closing it into a hum and without letting it end in a breathy 'h'. Repeat it gently, aloud or in the mind. Rest in the open quality of the sound.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 90 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Sound a soft, plain 'a' on part of an out-breath, or sound it in the mind only. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The plain vowel 'a', without a closing hum or a breathy ending
attention.secondary: The open, wordless quality of the sound

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is one open vowel, 'a', sounded without closing into a hum and without trailing off into a breath.
points: no nasal closing, no breathy ending

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. The commentary's breath-retention reading is not taught; keep breathing naturally between sounds. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: At the End of the Out-Breathed 'Ḥ'

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 91: Aspiration (Y67 ~ C2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: varṇasya savisargasya visargāntaṃ citiṃ kuru | nirādhāreṇa cittena spṛśed brahma sanātanam ||
dharana.rendering: Place awareness at the end of the visarga of a syllable that carries a visarga (the out-breathed 'ḥ'); with a mind free of support, one touches the eternal brahman.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: Abhinavagupta (Tantrāloka 3.143) and a verse quoted by Śivopādhyāya identify visarga with the creative power (kaulikī śakti) from which the cosmos emanates; written as two dots after a letter, it is spoken as a soft 'ḥ'. Fixing the mind at the very end of that sound, the symbol of manifestation, the mind is detached from manifestation and slips into the void, steeped in the silence of brahman.

instruction: Softly sound 'aḥ' and rest attention at the exact point where the breathy 'ḥ' fades into silence.

method.text: Sound 'aḥ' softly on an out-breath, so that it ends in a gentle breathy 'ḥ'. Place awareness at the exact point where the 'ḥ' fades into silence, and rest there with the mind leaning on nothing.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 91 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural in-breath. On the out-breath, sound 'aḥ' softly and let the 'ḥ' trail away with the breath. A free breath between rounds. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The very end of the soft out-breathed 'ḥ'
attention.secondary: The supportless silence after it

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a syllable ending in a soft breath-sound, and the exact point where that breath-sound becomes silence.
points: its very end, where it becomes silence

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Keep the out-breath soft and unforced; take free breaths between rounds. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Oneself as Boundless Sky
sanskrit: vyomākāraṃ svam ātmānaṃ dhyāyed digbhir anāvṛtam

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 92: The nature of the sky (Y68 ~ B2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: vyomākāraṃ svam ātmānaṃ dhyāyed digbhir anāvṛtam | nirāśrayā citiḥ śaktiḥ svarūpaṃ darśayet tadā ||
dharana.rendering: Let one meditate on one's own self as having the form of the sky, unbounded by any direction; then the power of consciousness (citi), freed of all support, reveals its own nature.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: one concentrates on the Self as a vast sky, unlimited by any form, adjunct or direction; in that frame of mind the power of consciousness is free of thought-constructs and shines in its own nature. Singh classes it as śāktopāya.

instruction: Feel yourself as open sky, with no edge in any direction.

method.text: Feel yourself not as a body in space but as space itself: open sky, with no edge in any direction. Let every sense of boundary go. Rest as that openness.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)

title: Attention Gathered at the Point of a Prick

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 93: Piercing (Y69 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kiṃcid aṅgaṃ vibhidyādau tīkṣṇasūcyādinā tataḥ | tatraiva cetanāṃ yuktvā bhairave nirmalā gatiḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Having first pierced some part of the body with a sharp needle or the like, and then joining awareness to that very spot, there is a pure passage into Bhairava.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.

instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class. Never pierce or injure the body.

method.text: Classical method: piercing some part of the body with a sharp needle or the like, then joining awareness to that very spot, there is a pure passage into Bhairava.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Self-injury is never taught or encouraged. Do not pierce, prick or harm the body in any way. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
safety.observe_only_note: Observe-only. Piercing the skin risks injury and infection and is self-harm; it is never done in this school. If you have urges to hurt yourself, please reach out to someone you trust or a local support service.

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 94: There is no mind (Y70 ~ B3)

dharana.rendering: Let one contemplate: 'Within me there is no inner apparatus consisting of mind and the rest.' Through the absence of thought-constructs, one becomes free of them.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: when one is fully convinced through contemplation that one is not the psychic apparatus of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi) and ego (ahaṃkāra) with which one is always identified, the mind stops forming thought-constructs and one's essential nature, beyond them, is revealed as pure consciousness.

instruction: Reflect, 'there is no thinking apparatus within me', and rest as the awareness that remains.

method.text: Sit quietly and reflect: 'Within me there is no apparatus of mind, intellect and ego.' Let the habit of identifying with thinking loosen. Rest as the awareness that remains.

title: Seeing Through the Powers That Limit
sanskrit: māyā vimohinī nāma kalāyāḥ kalanaṃ sthitam

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 95: (not a yukti)
numbering_variants.wallis_grouping: Wallis marks verse 95 '(not a yukti)': he does not count it as a technique.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: māyā vimohinī nāma kalāyāḥ kalanaṃ sthitam | ityādidharmaṃ tattvānāṃ kalayan na pṛthag bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: 'Māyā is the one that bewilders; the function of kalā is limiting activity': contemplating in this way the characteristics of the principles (tattvas), one no longer remains separate.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: Abhinavagupta defines māyā as the power that veils the Self and shows diversity; through her coverings (kañcukas) she limits activity, knowledge, desire, time and causation. Knowing their functions, the yogī does not lose sight of the wholeness of reality and sees manifestation as Śiva's expression. Singh records a variant, kalayan nā pṛthag bhavet ('such a person becomes isolated, established in the Self'). Wallis counts this verse as 'not a yukti'.

instruction: Recognise how time, place, knowledge, ability and desire limit experience, and stop taking those limits as who you are.

method.text: Reflect on how experience is limited: by time, by place, by what one can do, by what one knows, by what one wants. Recognise each as a function, not as who you are. Let the sense of separation from the whole ease.

attention.secondary: Not feeling separate from the whole

title: Letting a Desire Return to Its Source

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 96: Let desire dissolve (Y71 ~ C2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: jhagitīcchāṃ samutpannām avalokya śamaṃ nayet | yata eva samudbhūtā tatas tatraiva līyate ||
dharana.rendering: Seeing a desire as it suddenly arises, let one bring it to rest; it dissolves back into the very place from which it arose.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: when the mind is turned inward and one sees the Self as distinct from desire, a mere play of the mind, desires dissolve like waves back into the sea. If another desire arises, shift attention from the desire to the underlying reality, the creative moment (unmeṣa) between two desires. Wallis: 'dispassionately observing a desire suddenly arising'.

instruction: Catch a desire as it arises, look at it without acting or fighting, and let it sink back.

method.text: When a desire arises (to check the phone, to eat, to move), catch it at the moment it appears. Look at it without acting and without fighting it. Let it settle back into where it came from, and notice the quiet there.

attention.secondary: Its sinking back into its source
