title: Who Am I Before Desire or Knowing Arise?
sanskrit: yadā mamecchā notpannā jñānaṃ vā kas tadāsmi vai

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 97: I am as I am (Y72 ~ B2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: yadā mamecchā notpannā jñānaṃ vā kas tadāsmi vai | tattvato 'haṃ tathābhūtas tallīnas tanmanā bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: 'When no desire, and no knowing, has arisen in me, who am I then? In truth I am that, just as it is.' Absorbed in that, one's mind becomes one with it.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the desire, knowledge and activity of the ego are not those of the essential Self; when one realises and practises contemplation of the Self as pure consciousness-bliss, one rises above the ego and is dissolved in the essential Self. Wallis: 'I am as I am'.

instruction: In a moment with no wanting and no thinking, ask 'who am I now?' and rest without answering in words.

method.text: Rest until there is a moment with no particular want and no particular thought. Ask quietly: 'Who am I now?' Do not answer in words. Rest in what is there, just as it is.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)

seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 97 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The state before any desire or knowing arises
attention.secondary: The question 'who am I then?' left open

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the moment just before any wanting or knowing arises, and the question of what one is there.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: Desire or Knowing Seen as the Self
sanskrit: icchāyām athavā jñāne jāte cittaṃ niveśayet

dharana.rendering: When a desire or a cognition has arisen, let one place the mind on it, with the mind on nothing else, regarding it as the Self; then comes the vision of reality.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.

instruction: When a desire or thought arises, ignore its object and rest attention in the desire or thought itself as your own energy.

title: Thoughts Belong to No One

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 99: Thoughts belong to no one (Y74 ~ B1)

dharana.rendering: All cognition is without cause, without support, and of the nature of error; in truth it belongs to no one. One who contemplates in this way, O beloved, is Śiva.

instruction: Watch thoughts come and go and see them as belonging to no one.

method.text: Watch thoughts and perceptions arise. Contemplate each as having no fixed cause, no solid basis, and no owner. Let them come and go as if in open space. Rest as the knowing in which they appear.

attention.secondary: Knowing itself, without a knower or a known

title: The Same Awareness in Every Body

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 100: Awareness in all beings (Y75 ~ B1)

dharana.rendering: The nature of consciousness is present in all bodies; there is no difference anywhere. Therefore one who contemplates everything as made of it conquers worldly becoming.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: Kṣemarāja quotes this verse on the first Śivasūtra and stresses that consciousness (caitanya) means not just knowing but also free activity; one who realises the same conscious Self in all beings, from Sadāśiva to the tiniest worm, acquires the consciousness of essential oneness (samatā) and is freed from the round of birth and death. Wallis: 'awareness in all beings'.

instruction: Recognise the same awareness that is in you in every other living being.

method.text: Feel the awareness in your own body. Then bring to mind others (people nearby, animals, any living being) and contemplate the same awareness in each, with no difference. Rest in that sameness.

attention.secondary: No difference in it anywhere

title: Stillness at the Heart of a Strong Emotion

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 101: Reality is that which remains (Y76 ~ C2)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kāmakrodhalobhamohamadamātsaryagocare | buddhiṃ nistimitāṃ kṛtvā tat tattvam avaśiṣyate ||
dharana.rendering: In the grip of desire, anger, greed, confusion, intoxication or envy, let one make the mind utterly still; then the reality underlying them alone remains.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: under a strong emotion, dissociate the mind from its object and concentrate on the emotion itself, neither accepting nor rejecting it, withdrawing inward like a tortoise into its shell; the passion is calmed 'like a charmed snake', and one touches the inner pulse (spanda). He calls this ātma-saṃkoca or śakti-saṃkoca. Wallis: make the mind still and soft right in the middle of the emotion; reality is what remains.

instruction: In a strong emotion, set aside its story and rest, still and soft, inside the feeling itself.

method.text: When a strong emotion arises (anger, craving, envy), set aside its object and story. Turn toward the feeling itself and let the mind become very still and soft inside it, neither acting on it nor pushing it away. Stay until only its bare energy, or quiet, remains.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 101 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The emotion itself, felt directly, with the mind held still and soft

title: The World as a Magic Show or a Painting

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 102: Like a painting (Y77 ~ B1)

dharana.rendering: Letting go of what abides in one's own body, contemplating 'I am everywhere' with a firm mind and a gaze that looks at nothing else, one becomes happy.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.

Śivopādhyāya distinguishes the two: here the contemplation is 'all this is myself', the awareness of Sadāśiva or Īśvara. Wallis: 'I am everywhere'.

instruction: Let go of being located in this body and contemplate steadily, 'I am everywhere.'

title: Knowing and Willing in Everything, and Attention to the Link

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 105: Consciousness in everything (Y80 ~ B3); verse 106: Pay attention to the connection (Y81 ~ B3)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 105 'Dharana 82' (agrees) but verse 106 'Dharana 83'. Singh and the same book's Session Two count verse 106 as part of dhāraṇā 82, not a separate dhāraṇā. Not followed.
numbering_variants.two_verses: Singh heads verses 105 and 106 as one dhāraṇā (82) and notes that 106 contains no separate dhāraṇā; Wallis counts them as two yuktis (Y80, Y81).

dharana.sanskrit_iast: ghaṭādau yac ca vijñānam icchādyaṃ vā mamāntare | naiva sarvagataṃ jātam bhāvayann iti sarvagaḥ || grāhyagrāhakasaṃvittiḥ sāmānyā sarvadehinām | yogināṃ tu viśeṣo 'sti sambandhe sāvadhānatā ||
dharana.rendering: (105) 'The knowing, willing and the rest that are in me are not in me alone; they arise in everything, in a pot and other things too': contemplating this, one becomes all-pervading. (106) The awareness of object and subject is common to all embodied beings; the yogīs' distinction is that they stay attentive to the relation between them.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: knowing (jñāna) and willing/acting (icchā, kriyā) are not the monopoly of human beings but common to everything; contemplating this, one sheds insularity and feels kinship with all. He quotes Abhinavagupta and Somānanda: 'I know as one with the jar'. Singh states that verse 106 contains no separate dhāraṇā; it reinforces 105 by naming the yogī's distinction: mindfulness of the witnessing awareness to which every object is related. Wallis counts the two verses as separate yuktis: 'consciousness in everything' (Y80) and 'pay attention to the connection' (Y81).

instruction: Recognise your own knowing and willing in everything around you, and stay aware of the link between knower and known.

method.text: Contemplate that the knowing and willing you feel in yourself are present in everything around you: a pot, a stone, a cloud. Then, as you look at any object, stay attentive to the link between you, the knower, and it, the known.

breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.secondary: The relation between the one who knows and what is known

the link between knower and known

beats.title: Geometry
beats.script: No shape to make. Sit with the eyes open or closed. The map is the same spark in you and in every object.

beats.title: Orientation
beats.script: Let the floor or the chair carry you. Eyes closed or soft.

beats.title: Breath
beats.script: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps. No forced hold.

beats.title: Attention
beats.script: Feel your own knowing and willing. See the same in the pot, the stone, the cloud. Then stay aware of the link between you and what you see.

beats.title: Reaction cue

beats.title: Adiyogi thread
beats.script: Verse 105–106: the knowing and willing in me are in all things, even a pot; contemplating so, one becomes all-pervading. The yogī stays attentive to the link between knower and known.

beats.title: Exit / integrate
beats.script: Let the breath go unwatched for a round. Move the fingers and toes. Return to the room.

title: The Same Awareness in Another's Body

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 107: Becoming all-pervasive (Y82 ~ B3)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 107 'Dharana 84', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 83. Not followed.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: svavad anyaśarīre 'pi saṃvittim anubhāvayet | apekṣāṃ svaśarīrasya tyaktvā vyāpī dinair bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: Let one feel awareness in another's body just as in one's own; letting go of concern for one's own body, one becomes all-pervading within days.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: a body is not necessary for consciousness; in dream one is conscious apart from the gross body, in deep sleep apart from the subtle body, and in the fourth state apart from the causal body. Knowing this, one contemplates one's consciousness as not confined to one's own body. Wallis: 'cultivate the felt-sense that the consciousness in another's body is the same as one's own'.

instruction: Feel awareness alive in another person's body just as in your own.

method.text: Feel the awareness alive in your own body. Then bring to mind someone nearby, or a person you know, and feel the same awareness alive in their body, just as vividly. Let go of concern for your own body for a while.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 107 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: Awareness felt in another person's body as vividly as in one's own
attention.secondary: Releasing preoccupation with one's own body

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is awareness felt in one's own body and then, just as vividly, in another's.
points: the same awareness felt in another's body
concern for one's own body released

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Stay respectful: this is an inner contemplation, never a reason to cross anyone's physical or emotional boundaries. The verse's 'within days' is its own claim, not a promise. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

dharana.rendering: Making the mind supportless, let one not construct thought-constructs; then, O doe-eyed one, in the self becoming the supreme self, there is Bhairava.

instruction: Let the mind rest on nothing, and do not build on any thought that appears.

method.text: Let the mind rest on nothing: no object, no image, no idea. When a thought appears, do not build on it; let it pass. Rest in the open awareness that remains.

title: Whirling Until Falling (Classical)

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 111: Cessation of the energy of excitation (Y86 ~ C1)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: bhrāntvā bhrāntvā śarīreṇa tvaritam bhuvi pātanāt | kṣobhaśaktivirāmeṇa parā saṃjāyate daśā ||
dharana.rendering: Whirling the body round and round, then swiftly falling to the ground: through the cessation of the energy of agitation, the supreme state arises.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh comments on verses 111 and 112 together: both refer to the condition of mind at the end of an intense commotion, here physical, in 112 intellectual. When the stirring ceases, thought-constructs are laid to rest and Bhairava's nature is revealed. He classes 111 as śāmbhavopāya. Wallis: 'cessation of the energy of excitation'.

instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class. Never spin until falling. For a gentle practice of stillness after movement, use Door 060.

method.text: Classical method: whirling the body round and round and then swiftly falling to the ground, the supreme state arises through the cessation of the energy of agitation.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

safety.observe_only_note: Observe-only. Spinning until you fall can cause falls, head and joint injuries, nausea and fainting, and is unsafe with heart, blood-pressure, inner-ear or balance conditions and in pregnancy. For a gentle practice of stillness after movement, use Door 060.

title: When the Mind Gives Up: The Stillness After an Impasse

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 112: The power of incapacity (Y87 ~ C2)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 112 'Dharana 89', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 88. Not followed.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: ādhāreṣv athavā 'śaktyā 'jñānāc cittalayena vā | jātaśaktisamāveśakṣobhānte bhairavaṃ vapuḥ ||
dharana.rendering: Or, through inability regarding the supports (of knowing), or through the dissolution of the mind from not-knowing, at the end of the agitation of the absorption that arises, there is Bhairava's form.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: through lack of power to apprehend objects of knowledge, or through sheer ignorance, the mind dissolves; at the end of the commotion this brings, Bhairava's nature appears. With verse 111, it describes the mind at the end of intense commotion: here a commotion of intellectual impasse, as when obstinate questioning or doubt exhausts itself. Singh classes it as śāktopāya. Wallis: 'the power of incapacity', incapacity regarding the loci (ādhāras).

instruction: When the mind cannot grasp or solve something, stop pushing and rest in the stillness after the struggle.

method.text: When the mind meets something it cannot grasp (a question with no answer, a problem it cannot solve), stop pushing. Let the not-knowing be complete. As the agitation of effort subsides, notice the stillness that remains, and rest in it.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 112 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The moment the mind gives up trying to grasp or solve something
attention.secondary: The stillness that follows when the agitation subsides

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a mind pushing against a wall it cannot pass, then the quiet when it stops pushing.
points: the effort to know or solve
the impasse, where the mind cannot go on

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. This is about letting go of mental effort, not about ignoring practical problems; return to them afterwards with a rested mind. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

beats.script: No shape to make. Sit or lie down. The map is a mind pushing against a wall, then the quiet when it stops.

beats.title: Orientation
beats.script: Let the floor or the chair carry you. Eyes closed or soft.

beats.title: Breath
beats.script: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps. No forced hold.

beats.title: Attention
beats.script: Bring to mind a question with no answer. Notice the push to solve it. Let the push stop. Rest in the quiet after.

beats.script: School image: a mind ceasing to push. A metaphor, not medicine.

beats.title: Adiyogi thread
beats.script: Verse 112: through inability regarding the supports of knowing, or the mind dissolving in not-knowing, at the end of that agitation there is Bhairava's form.

beats.title: Exit / integrate
beats.script: Let the practice go. Take one free breath. Open the eyes and look around the room.

title: Unmoving Eyes; Ears and Lower Openings Closed (Classical)
sanskrit: netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayoḥ … saṃkocaṃ karṇayoḥ kṛtvā hy adhodvāre

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 113: Eyes ‘paralyzed’ (Y88 ~ C1); verse 114: Blocking the ears and hearing the unstruck sound (Y89 ~ A2)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 113 'Dharana 90', verse 114 'Dharana 91', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 89. Not followed.
numbering_variants.two_verses: Singh heads verses 113 and 114 together as one dhāraṇā; Wallis counts them as two yuktis (Y88, Y89).

dharana.sanskrit_iast: sampradāyam imam devi śṛṇu samyag vadāmy aham | kaivalyaṃ jāyate sadyo netrayoḥ stabdhamātrayoḥ || saṃkocaṃ karṇayoḥ kṛtvā hy adhodvāre tathaiva ca | anackam ahalaṃ dhyāyan viśed brahma sanātanam ||
dharana.rendering: (113) O Goddess, listen: I shall tell you this tradition fully. For one whose eyes are held motionless, aloneness-in-freedom (kaivalya) arises at once. (114) Contracting the ears, and the lower opening likewise, meditating on the unstruck sound without vowel or consonant, one enters the eternal brahman.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the unmoving eyes refer to the bhairavī mudrā, eyes open outward without blinking while attention turns to the reality within; he cites Kṣemarāja's Svacchanda Tantra commentary. In 114, the openings of the ears and of the anus and genital are contracted and one meditates on the inner, unstruck sound (anāhata) without vowel or consonant; he relates it to bindu (Śiva) and pure visarga (Śakti). He stresses that kaivalya here is not Sāṃkhya isolation but the world contracted into Śiva. Wallis counts the verses as two yuktis: 'eyes paralyzed' (Y88) and 'blocking the ears and hearing the unstruck sound' (Y89).

instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class. Do not hold an unblinking gaze, press the ears, or contract the pelvic openings from this door. For gentle related practices, use Door 066 or Door 017.

method.text: Classical method: with the eyes held motionless, aloneness-in-freedom arises at once; contracting the ears and the lower opening, and meditating on the unstruck sound without vowel or consonant, one enters the eternal brahman.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. No sustained unblinking gaze, no pressing on the ears and no pelvic contractions are taught from this door. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
safety.observe_only_note: Observe-only. A sustained unblinking gaze can dry and strain the eyes, pressing the ears can hurt them, and sustained pelvic contractions belong to lineage training and can strain the pelvic floor. For gentle related practices, use Door 066 (gently quieting a sense) or Door 017 (listening into silence).

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kūpādike mahāgarte sthitvopari nirīkṣaṇāt | avikalpamateḥ samyak sadyaś cittalayaḥ sphuṭam ||
dharana.rendering: Standing above a well or some great chasm and gazing down into it, for one whose understanding is free of thought-constructs, the dissolution of the mind clearly happens at once.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh adds 'without blinking' in brackets: if the yogī gazes for a long time into the space of a deep well, or from a high summit, he feels giddiness and fear, and the inner pulse (spanda) throws him out of ordinary consciousness; if his intuitive understanding is pure, it is freed of thought-constructs and he knows surpassing peace. He classes it as śāmbhavopāya. Wallis: 'gazing into a well' (deep well, chasm or the like).

instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class. Never stand over a drop to gaze down. For safe gazing practices, use Door 036 or Door 061.

method.text: Classical method: standing above a deep well or chasm and gazing down into it, the mind of one free of thought-constructs dissolves at once.
method.note: Historical / observe only. Read and understood, not practised. No practice cues are given for this door.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. Do not stand at edges, wells, cliffs or heights to practise. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
safety.observe_only_note: Observe-only. Standing over a drop and gazing down deliberately provokes vertigo and fear and risks a fall. For a safe practice of gazing into open space, use Door 036 (the space inside a pot) or Door 061 (a clear sky).

title: Wherever the Mind Goes

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 116: Wherever the mind goes (Y91 ~ B1)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 116 'Dharana 93', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 91. Not followed.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: yatra yatra mano yāti bāhye vābhyantare 'pi vā | tatra tatra śivāvasthā vyāpakatvāt kva yāsyati ||
dharana.rendering: Wherever the mind goes, outward or inward, there is the state of Śiva; since it pervades everything, where could the mind go?
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: metaphysically, everything subjective or objective is Śiva; in practice, the aspirant need not struggle to concentrate on some mysterious reality. Whatever attracts the mind, outer (a jar, a colour) or inner (an emotion, a thought), is taken with full conviction as Śiva and meditated on; it then appears as universal consciousness in that form. He links it to Spandakārikā 2.3–5. Wallis: 'wherever the mind goes'.

instruction: Wherever the mind wanders, outside or inside, take that very place as the sacred and rest there.

method.text: Let the mind go where it goes: a sound, a colour, a memory, a feeling. Do not pull it back. Wherever it lands, take that as the state of Śiva and rest there, until it moves on, and do the same again.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 116 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: Wherever the mind lands, outer or inner
attention.secondary: That very place taken as the state of Śiva

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the mind wandering in every direction and finding the same reality wherever it lands.

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

instruction: Feel each sound, sight and touch as consciousness itself appearing, like an image that is only the mirror.

title: Sneezes, Shocks and Sudden Moments

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kṣutādyante bhaye śoke gahvare vā raṇād drute | kutūhale kṣudhādyante brahmasattāmayī daśā ||

He cites Spandakārikā 1.22 (extreme anger, joy, impasse, flight for one's life). Singh classes it as śāmbhavopāya. Wallis: 'the intensity of the moment'; Bäumer and Dyczkowski take gahvara as a deep pit or abyss.

instruction: When a sneeze, a pang of hunger or a sudden surprise comes, notice the brief opening it makes.

method.text: In daily life, notice moments that jolt ordinary awareness: the instant before and after a sneeze, the start or end of hunger, a sudden surprise, a flash of curiosity, the first moment of fear or sorrow. instruction: At a familiar place, let its memories go and see it fresh, with the body feeling open and unsupported.

title: Placing the Gaze, Then Withdrawing It
sanskrit: kvacid vastuni vinyasya śanair dṛṣṭiṃ nivartayet

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 120: Yogic withdrawal (Y95 ~ A3)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 120 'Dharana 97', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 95. Not followed.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: kvacid vastuni vinyasya śanair dṛṣṭiṃ nivartayet | taj jñānaṃ cittasahitaṃ devi śūnyālayo bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: Having placed the gaze on some object, let one slowly withdraw it, and with it the knowledge of the object, together with the mind; O Goddess, one becomes a dwelling of the void.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the knowledge and impression of the object can be eliminated either through contemplating the world as void (śūnya-bhāvanā) or through the bhairavī mudrā, eyes open without blinking but attention turned to the Self; either way the external world loses its hold. He classes it as śāktopāya. Wallis: 'yogic withdrawal': fix the gaze, slowly withdraw it, then the thought of it, then the heart-mind itself.

instruction: Rest the gaze on one object, then slowly withdraw the gaze, the thought of the object and the mind into emptiness.

method.text: Rest your gaze on one simple object. Then, slowly, withdraw it: let the eyes soften or close, let the thought of the object fade, and let the mind itself settle back, until only open emptiness remains. Rest there.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 120 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The gaze resting on one simple object
attention.secondary: The slow withdrawal of the gaze, then of the thought of the object, then of the mind, into emptiness

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the gaze going out to one object and slowly returning, bringing the knowing of the object back with it into emptiness.
points: the gaze, the knowledge and the mind slowly withdrawn

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

title: The Understanding Born of Devotion

dharana.sanskrit_iast: bhaktyudrekād viraktasya yādṛśī jāyate matiḥ | sā śaktiḥ śāṅkarī nityam bhavayet tāṃ tataḥ śivaḥ ||
dharana.rendering: The kind of understanding (mati) that arises from an overflowing of devotion in one who is free of attachment is the power of Śaṅkara (Śiva); let one contemplate it constantly, and then one is Śiva.

Devotion, he says, is not just presenting flowers and incense but seeing God in all life and dedicating oneself in word, thought and deed. Singh classes it as śāmbhavopāya. Wallis: 'intense devotion'.

instruction: Let devotion well up without grasping, and keep returning to the clear understanding it brings.

attention.secondary: The quiet understanding that arises from it, contemplated again and again

title: While One Thing Is Known, the Emptiness of All Others

dharana.sanskrit_iast: vastvantare vedyamāne sarvavastuṣu śūnyatā | tām eva manasā dhyātvā vidito 'pi praśāmyati ||
dharana.rendering: While one particular object is being perceived, there is emptiness with regard to all other things; meditating with the mind on that very emptiness, even though the object is still known, one becomes calm.

dharana.rendering: The purity that people of slight understanding uphold is impurity in Śiva's teaching; it is not purity but impurity. Therefore, free of thought-constructs, one becomes happy.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.

Real purity is freedom from thought-constructs, and only that brings happiness. Singh reports Lakshmanjoo's reading na śucir nāśucis: 'it is neither purity nor impurity'; Wallis's translation follows it.

instruction: See your ideas of pure and impure as constructs of the mind, and set them down.

method.text: Notice where you divide experience into pure and impure, clean and unclean, worthy and unworthy. See those divisions as constructs of the mind. Set them down, and rest in the ease that follows.

attention.secondary: The ease of not dividing experience that way

attention.secondary: The awakening that arises at the end of that contemplation

title: Wherever the Mind Goes, Let It Go at Once
sanskrit: yatra yatra mano yāti tat tat tenaiva tatkṣaṇam

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 129: Nothing to hang onto (Y104 ~ C3)

dharana.sanskrit_iast: yatra yatra mano yāti tat tat tenaiva tatkṣaṇam | parityajyānavasthityā nistaraṅgas tato bhavet ||
dharana.rendering: Wherever the mind goes, let it give up that very thing, in that very instant, by that same mind; by not settling anywhere, one becomes free of waves.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: agitation of mind is removed by dispassion and practice together: the negative method withdraws attention from whatever distracts it, the positive method concentrates on the object of meditation. He cites Bhagavad Gītā 6.26. Wallis: 'nothing to hang onto'; having nothing to hang onto, the mind becomes 'waveless'. The verse opens with the same words as verse 116 (D-091), but there the mind's destination is embraced; here it is released.

instruction: Wherever the mind lands, let it go in that same instant, and do not let it settle anywhere.

method.text: Watch where the mind goes: a sound, a thought, an itch. In the very instant it lands, let it go, using the same mind that went there. Do not let it settle anywhere. Notice the stillness that grows.

attention.secondary: The waveless mind that remains

title: Sounding the Name 'Bhairava'

dharana.sanskrit_iast: bhayā sarvaṃ ravayati sarvado vyāpako 'khile | iti bhairavaśabdasya santatoccāraṇāc chivaḥ ||

dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh gives several traditional etymologies of 'Bhairava': bhā (the light of consciousness) + ai (the power of action) + rava (comprehending); Abhinavagupta's 'he who supports the cosmos and sounds the great mantra I (aham)'; bha-ra-va as maintenance, withdrawal and projection of the universe. He insists that uccāra here is not mechanical repetition but the sounding of the inner life-force (prāṇa-śakti) rising from the heart to the dvādaśānta. Singh classes it as śāktopāya. Wallis notes there are up to five ways to translate the verse.

instruction: Softly and steadily sound 'Bhairava', aloud or silently, remembering its meaning.

method.text: Recall the meaning: radiance that makes everything resound, that gives all, that pervades all. Then sound 'Bhai-ra-va' softly and steadily, aloud or in the mind, with that meaning in the sound, not as a mechanical repetition.

title: 'I' and 'Mine': Following Them to No Support

numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 131 'Dharana 108', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). dharana.sanskrit_iast: ahaṃ mamedam ityādi pratipattiprasaṅgataḥ | nirādhāre mano yāti taddhyānapreraṇāc chamī ||
dharana.rendering: On the occasion of thoughts like 'I am', 'this is mine', the mind goes to what has no support; impelled by contemplating that, one becomes peaceful.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the supportless is the absolute 'I' (pūrṇāham), free of thought-constructs, present behind the everyday 'I' in the ignorant and the wise alike; whenever one says 'I', the mind subconsciously reflects it, and contemplating that thought-free 'I' as one's real Self, a pure thought ends in thought-free awareness (citing Tantrāloka 1.214–215). He classes it as śāktopāya. Wallis: when you hear yourself say 'I am…' or 'this is mine', inquire what 'I' or 'my' refers to; the mind looks for a referent and cannot find one.

instruction: When you think 'I' or 'mine', ask what it refers to, and rest in the open awareness you find.

method.text: When you notice yourself thinking or saying 'I am…' or 'this is mine', pause. Ask what the 'I' refers to. Let the mind look, and when it finds nothing solid, rest in that open, supportless awareness.

attention.secondary: The supportless awareness they point back to

title: All This Is Like a Magic Show

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 133: All this is a magic show (Y108 ~ B2)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 133 'Dharana 110', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 108. Not followed.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: atattvam indrajālābham idaṃ sarvam avasthitam | kiṃ tattvam indrajālasya iti dārḍhyāc chamaṃ vrajet ||
dharana.rendering: 'This whole world stands without essential reality, like a magic show; what reality does a magic show have?' Through firmness in this, one attains peace.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh comments on verses 133 and 134 together: both concern the unreality of the world; 133 says the world is like a magic show and therefore has no reality, and contemplating so, one acquires peace. Wallis: 'all this is a magic show'. Compare verse 102 (D-079), where seeing the world as a magic show brings happiness.

instruction: Hold firmly the view that all this is like a magic show, and let peace settle in.

method.text: Look at what appears (events, objects, your own roles) and ask: how real is a magic show? Hold the view firmly that all this, however vivid, is like a magic show, and let the peace of that settle in.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 133 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The world seen as a magic show, without essential reality
attention.secondary: Peace through firmly holding that view

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the world as a stage show: vivid, convincing, and without solid reality behind it.
points: the peace of not taking it as solid

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. This view is for loosening inner grip, not for dismissing responsibility or anyone's suffering. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

title: The Unchanging Self: This World Is Empty
sanskrit: ātmano nirvikārasya kva jñānaṃ kva ca vā kriyā

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 134: The world is ‘empty’ (not a yukti)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 134 'Dharana 111', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 109. Not followed.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: ātmano nirvikārasya kva jñānaṃ kva ca vā kriyā | jñānāyattā bahirbhāvā ataḥ śūnyam idaṃ jagat ||
dharana.rendering: In the unchanging Self, where is knowing and where is acting? External things depend on knowing; therefore this world is empty.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh (on 133–134 together): the Self is one mass of consciousness without change; knowing and acting, in the sense of the limited individual's changing, difference-ridden knowing and acting, cannot belong to it, and external objects depend on them, so the world is empty; contemplating so, one acquires peace. The knowing and acting that belong to the Self are its powers (jñāna-śakti, kriyā-śakti), not dependent on mind or senses. Wallis counts verse 134 as 'not a yukti'.

instruction: Rest as the unchanging awareness behind all knowing and doing, and see the world as empty.

method.text: Notice that knowing and doing keep changing, while the awareness in which they appear does not. Rest as that unchanging awareness. See the world, which depends on being known, as empty of solid reality.

attention.secondary: The world, which depends on knowing, seen as empty

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a still centre that does not change, with the moving world of knowing and doing seen as empty around it.
points: the world that depends on them, seen as empty

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

title: No Bondage, No Liberation: The Sun in the Water
sanskrit: na me bandho na mokṣo me

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 135: Reflections in the mind (Y109 ~ B3)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 135 'Dharana 112', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 110. Not followed.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: na me bandho na mokṣo me bhītasyaitā vibhīṣikāḥ | pratibimbam idam buddher jaleṣv iva vivasvataḥ ||
dharana.rendering: 'For me there is no bondage and no liberation; these are bogeys for the frightened. This world is a reflection in the intellect, like the sun in water.'
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the Self is pure consciousness, unlimited by space and time, so bondage and liberation can arise only for what is limited; just as the sun's image appears inverted in water, it is the limited intellect (buddhi), reflecting the Self, that passes itself off as the Self and thinks itself bound or freed. He cites Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñā-vimarśinī. Singh reports that Lakshmanjoo prefers jīvasya ('for the embodied individual') to bhītasya ('for the frightened'). Singh classes it as śāmbhavopāya. Wallis: 'reflections in the mind'.

instruction: Picture the sun in water and contemplate, 'for me there is neither bondage nor liberation.'

method.text: Picture the sun reflected in several pools of water. The reflections ripple and break; the sun is untouched. Contemplate: 'For me there is no bondage and no liberation.' Rest as the sun, not the reflection.

attention.secondary: The world as a reflection, like the sun in water

title: Pleasure and Pain Come Through the Senses: Abiding in Oneself

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 136: Abide in oneself (Y110 ~ C3)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 136 'Dharana 113', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). dharana.sanskrit_iast: indriyadvārakaṃ sarvaṃ sukhaduḥkhādisaṃgamam | itīndriyāṇi saṃtyajya svasthaḥ svātmani vartate ||
dharana.rendering: All contact with pleasure, pain and the rest comes through the doors of the senses; knowing this, letting go of the senses, one abides at ease in one's own Self.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: pleasure and pain received through the senses belong not to the essential Self but to the psycho-physical complex; this is achieved mainly by śakti-saṃkoca, which the Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya defines as turning back toward the Self the consciousness spreading outward through the senses. One becomes poised in oneself (svastha), free of the opposites. He cites the Yogavāsiṣṭha. Singh classes it as śāktopāya. Wallis: 'abide in oneself'; let go of attachment to the senses and be at ease in the natural state.

instruction: Notice that pleasure and pain come through the senses, and let attention turn back to rest at ease within.

method.text: Notice that every pleasant or unpleasant experience arrives through a sense: seeing, hearing, touch, taste, smell. Without closing anything off, let attention stop reaching out through those doors and turn back. Rest, at ease, in yourself.

attention.secondary: Attention resting at ease in oneself, not reaching out through them

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the senses as doors through which pleasure and pain arrive, and attention turning back from the doors to rest at home.

title: Knower and Known as One

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 137: One essential nature (Y111 ~ B3)
numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 137 'Dharana 114', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 112. Not followed.
numbering_variants.prototype_seed: The older prototype seed doors/112.json pairs door 112 with verse 138, Wallis yukti 112 (superseded: under Singh, dhāraṇā 112 is verse 137; Singh reads verse 138 as the conclusion that follows the 112 dhāraṇās). Not followed.

dharana.sanskrit_iast: jñānaprakāśakaṃ sarvaṃ sarveṇātmā prakāśakaḥ | ekam ekasvabhāvatvāj jñānaṃ jñeyaṃ vibhāvyate ||
dharana.rendering: Everything is revealed by knowing, and the Self is revealed by everything; because their nature is one, knowing and the known are contemplated as one.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: 'knowing' here stands for the knower; the known is revealed by the knower and the knower by the known. He cites the Ucchuṣmabhairava ('so long as there are no knowers, how can there be the known?') and a verse quoted by Śivopādhyāya: manifestation is not separate from the light of consciousness, nor that light from I-consciousness. Contemplating subject, object and consciousness as one reality, one attains Bhairava's nature. Singh classes it as śāktopāya. Singh reports a second reading, per Lakshmanjoo: 'knowledge reveals things in the world and the Self is the source of all revelation; since they are not different, the knower is revealed in knowledge'. Wallis's translation follows that reading.

instruction: Notice that what you know and the one who knows reveal each other, and rest in them as one knowing.

method.text: Look at, or listen to, anything. Notice that it is revealed by your knowing, and that your knowing is revealed by it. Let the two be seen as one nature, one knowing, and rest there.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 137 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

attention.primary: The knower and the known, each revealing the other
attention.secondary: Their single shared nature: knowing

attention_map.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the knower and the known as two faces of one knowing, each revealing the other.
points: knowing, which is the same nature in both

notes: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.

General practice caution only; not medical advice. If this becomes abstract, simply rest in plain seeing or hearing. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.

honesty.disclosure: Door 112 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 112 (verse 137) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
flags: Door index = Jaideva Singh dharana number: Door 112 is dharana 112, verse 137. Other editions number differently (see dharana.numbering_variants).
The seat, breath counts, reaction metaphor, attention-map drawing and beat scripts are school devices, not part of the verse.
The English is a school paraphrase, not a quotation from any translator.
No medical claims. Reaction names are metaphors, not biochemistry.

beats.title: Name the door
beats.script: This is Door 112: knower and known as one. Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 112, verse 137.

beats.title: Geometry
beats.script: No shape to make. Sit with the eyes open or closed. The map is the knower and the known as one knowing.

beats.title: Orientation
beats.script: Let the floor or the chair carry you. Eyes closed or soft.

beats.title: Breath
beats.script: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps. No forced hold.

beats.title: Attention
beats.script: Look at anything. It is revealed by your knowing; your knowing is revealed by it. One nature. Rest there.

beats.title: Reaction cue
beats.script: School image: two arcs closing into one circle. A metaphor, not medicine.

beats.title: Adiyogi thread
beats.script: Verse 137: everything is revealed by knowing, and the Self by everything; because their nature is one, knower and known are contemplated as one.

beats.title: Exit / integrate
beats.script: Let the practice go. Take one free breath. Open the eyes and look around the room.
